subjectWideQuestions.stem: A physician orders "PSG with extended EEG montage." Compared with standard PSG EEG, the extended montage typically includes:

options.text: Only two EEG channels instead of the standard three.
The same three EEG channels as standard PSG.
Additional EEG electrodes covering more scalp regions (e.g., F3, F4, C3, C4, O1, O2, and possibly temporal leads), beyond the standard minimum of three derivations.
Invasive depth electrodes placed by a neurosurgeon.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Standard PSG EEG montage uses a minimum of three derivations: frontal (F4-M1), central (C4-M1), and occipital (O2-M1). An "extended EEG montage" adds electrodes to cover additional brain regions — typically the homologous left-sided electrodes (F3, C3, O1) plus possibly temporal leads (T3, T4) and/or additional frontal/parietal placements. The purpose is usually to evaluate for seizure activity, parasomnias, or other neurological conditions that require broader spatial sampling. The extended montage still uses surface electrodes; invasive depth electrodes are a neurosurgical procedure done in an epilepsy monitoring unit, not a sleep lab.

**Clue in the question.** "Extended EEG montage" — "extended" means more channels than standard, not fewer and not invasive. The distinction from standard (3 derivations) to extended (6-16+ derivations) is the core concept.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Extended EEG montage for PSG.
rationales.eli10:
A basic sleep study uses three brain wave sensors (front, middle, and back of the head, all on the right side). But sometimes doctors need more information — maybe they're looking for seizure activity or unusual sleep behaviors. An "extended" EEG setup means adding more sensors: covering the left side of the head too, and maybe adding some on the sides (temples). It's the same type of stickers, just more of them spread across more of the head for a wider view.

ELI Example

Standard EEG is like a 3-camera security system covering the front door, living room, and back door. Extended EEG is like a 10-camera system that also covers side windows, garage, and basement — same technology, just more coverage for a more complete picture.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Extended montage means MORE channels, not fewer. Two channels would be below even the standard minimum. Extended implies additional coverage beyond standard.

**B.** The same three channels as standard PSG is, by definition, not "extended." The order specifically requests more than standard.

**D.** Invasive depth electrodes require burr holes drilled through the skull by a neurosurgeon — this is an epilepsy surgery procedure, not a PSG technologist task. Extended PSG EEG uses surface electrodes only.

Exam Trap

Confusing "extended EEG montage" (more surface electrodes, within technologist scope) with invasive EEG monitoring (depth/grid electrodes, neurosurgical procedure). The technologist applies surface electrodes only.

Memory Anchor

Extended EEG = more surface electrodes (bilateral, temporal) beyond standard 3 derivations. Still surface electrodes. Still within technologist scope. NOT invasive/surgical.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The 60 Hz notch filter is enabled on all EEG channels during diagnostic recording. Per AASM recommendations, notch filter use during PSG is:

options.text: Required for all PSG recordings.
Required only during CPAP titration.
Never permitted under any circumstances.

Discouraged for routine use because it can attenuate clinically important activity in the 50-60 Hz range, and should be reserved for cases where 60 Hz interference cannot be eliminated by correcting impedances, lead placement, or environmental factors.

rationales.whyCorrect:
The 60 Hz notch filter is a narrow-band filter that specifically attenuates 60 Hz (and often harmonics). While it effectively removes electrical line noise, AASM guidelines discourage its routine use because: (1) clinically important EEG activity exists in the 50-60 Hz range (high beta, gamma activity, muscle artifact that helps identify arousals, and certain epileptiform discharges have fast components); (2) notch filters can produce "ringing" artifacts (oscillations) after sharp transients; (3) using a notch filter masks underlying technical problems (poor impedances, bad lead routing) that should be corrected instead of electronically covered up. The recommended approach is to identify and ELIMINATE the source of 60 Hz interference through proper skin preparation, matched low impedances, twisted lead wires, and removal of nearby electrical noise sources.

**Clue in the question.** "AASM recommendations" and "notch filter use during PSG" — the guidelines specifically address this as an issue of signal integrity vs. convenience.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Notch filter use per AASM recommendations.
rationales.eli10:
The 60 Hz notch filter is like putting earplugs in to block out a humming sound — it gets rid of the hum, but it also blocks some things you WANT to hear. Instead of using the filter, the better approach is to find and fix what's causing the hum: check that all the sensor connections are good, keep wires away from power cords, and make sure the skin preparation is done right. Fix the problem at its source rather than filtering out the symptom (and some real brain signals along with it).

ELI Example

Like using noise-canceling headphones to block traffic noise while trying to listen for birdsong — the headphones might cancel the traffic, but they'll also cancel the birdsong that's at the same pitch. Better solution: close the window (eliminate the noise source) so you can hear everything clearly.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Notch filters are NOT required for all PSG recordings. In fact, AASM discourages routine use. A well-prepared recording should not need a notch filter.

**B.** Notch filters are not specifically required during CPAP titration. The same principle applies regardless of study type — fix the interference, don't filter it.

**C.** Notch filters ARE permitted when 60 Hz cannot be eliminated by other means. The guideline says "discouraged for routine use" and "reserved for refractory cases," not "never permitted." There are clinical situations where the benefit of reducing severe 60 Hz artifact outweighs the signal loss.

Exam Trap

Assuming that because notch filters exist and work, they should always be used. The exam tests whether you understand the clinical trade-off: a notch filter removes artifact but also removes real brain activity in the same frequency band.

Memory Anchor

60 Hz notch filter = discouraged for routine use per AASM. Fix the source (impedances, lead routing, environment) first. Use notch filter only as last resort when interference cannot be eliminated.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During PSG, SpO2 drops from 95% to 68% over 15 seconds and the pulse waveform becomes erratic. Respiratory effort and airflow continue. The technologist should FIRST:

options.text: Increase CPAP pressure to maximum.
Call a code blue immediately.
Wake the patient and terminate the study.
Go to the patient's room to check sensor placement and clinical status, as a rapid drop of this magnitude may indicate sensor displacement rather than true desaturation.

rationales.whyCorrect:
A drop from 95% to 68% over 15 seconds is both too rapid and too extreme to be a true physiological desaturation in a patient with continued respiratory effort and airflow. Hemoglobin desaturation during apnea typically occurs over 30-90 seconds, not 15 seconds. The combination of a precipitous drop, erratic pulse waveform, and continued respiratory effort strongly suggests sensor displacement — the oximeter probe has partially fallen off or shifted, causing loss of adequate photoplethysmographic signal. The correct first action is to physically check the patient and the sensor. If the patient is clinically stable and the sensor is displaced, repositioning resolves the "desaturation" immediately. If the patient truly has SpO2 of 68%, clinical signs (cyanosis, altered mental status, respiratory distress) would be obvious and require immediate intervention.

**Clue in the question.** "SpO2 drops from 95% to 68% over 15 seconds" with "respiratory effort and airflow continue" — the speed of the drop is physiologically impossible for true desaturation with ongoing ventilation.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify/Respond/Document: Acute SpO2 change during PSG.
rationales.eli10:
If a patient's oxygen level suddenly drops from normal to dangerously low in just 15 seconds while they're still breathing, the most likely explanation isn't a medical emergency — it's that the finger sensor has slipped off or moved. Real oxygen drops during sleep apnea happen gradually over 30 seconds to a minute or more. The first thing to do is go check: is the patient actually in trouble, or did the sensor just fall off? Nine times out of ten, it's a sensor problem.

ELI Example

If your car's temperature gauge suddenly shoots from normal to "overheating" in 5 seconds while you're cruising on the highway, you don't immediately pull over and call a tow truck — you suspect the gauge is broken, because engines don't overheat that fast. The SpO2 sensor works similarly: unbelievable speed = unbelievable reading = check the sensor first.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Increasing CPAP to maximum without first verifying that the desaturation is real and obstructive in origin is dangerous and inappropriate. If the patient is on a diagnostic study (no CPAP), this option is impossible. Even on CPAP, treating a sensor artifact as a respiratory event can cause harm.

**B.** Calling a code blue without first assessing the patient is inappropriate. A code blue should be called for cardiac or respiratory arrest, not for an oximeter reading. Assessment always precedes emergency activation.

**C.** Waking the patient and terminating the study is premature before verifying whether the reading is real. If it's sensor displacement, waking the patient unnecessarily disrupts the study and causes patient distress.

Exam Trap

Reacting to monitor numbers without first assessing the patient. The classic teaching: "Treat the patient, not the monitor." The exam tests whether you verify alarming data with direct patient assessment before escalating.

Memory Anchor

Rapid extreme SpO2 drop (seconds) + continued breathing + erratic waveform = sensor displacement. Check sensor and patient BEFORE escalating.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: When configuring the amplifier for standard diagnostic PSG, the recommended low-frequency filter (high-pass) for EEG channels is:

options.text: 0.1 Hz, to capture infra-slow oscillations.
1.0 Hz, to eliminate sweat artifact while preserving delta.
0.3 Hz, to preserve slow-wave EEG activity while attenuating slower baseline drift.
3.0 Hz, to eliminate all slow-frequency artifact.

rationales.whyCorrect:
The AASM recommends a low-frequency filter (LFF, also called high-pass filter) setting of 0.3 Hz for EEG channels in standard PSG. This setting preserves clinically important delta activity (0.5-2 Hz), which is essential for identifying N3 slow-wave sleep and for detecting pathological slow-wave abnormalities. At the same time, a 0.3 Hz LFF attenuates very slow baseline drift (below 0.3 Hz) caused by sweat, slow electrode polarization changes, and patient movement. Setting the LFF higher (e.g., 1.0 Hz or 3.0 Hz) would progressively attenuate delta waves, making N3 sleep appear to have lower amplitude and potentially leading to underscoring of slow-wave sleep. Setting it lower (0.1 Hz) would allow excessive baseline wander that degrades signal quality without adding clinically useful information.

**Clue in the question.** "Recommended low-frequency filter (high-pass) for EEG channels" in standard PSG — this is a specific AASM technical specification.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: EEG filter settings for standard PSG.
rationales.eli10:
The EEG filter is like a camera lens that decides what to keep and what to blur. The low-frequency filter at 0.3 Hz says: "Keep everything faster than about 3 waves per 10 seconds, but blur out anything slower." This preserves the important deep-sleep brain waves (delta waves, about 0.5-2 waves per second) while getting rid of unwanted slow drift from sweat or slight movements. If you set the filter too high (1.0 or 3.0 Hz), you accidentally blur out the delta waves you're trying to see.

ELI Example

Like a sieve for sifting flour — you want holes that let the fine flour (delta waves) through but catch the big lumps (sweat artifact). 0.3 Hz is the right hole size: big enough for delta to pass, small enough to catch unwanted slow drift.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** 0.1 Hz preserves infra-slow oscillations but also allows excessive baseline wander from sweat, respiration, and movement — degrading signal quality. Infra-slow activity is not clinically scored in standard PSG.

**B.** 1.0 Hz would begin attenuating delta activity (0.5-2.0 Hz), particularly the slower delta components. This could cause underscoring of N3 sleep, which requires at least 20% delta activity per epoch.

**D.** 3.0 Hz would severely attenuate delta activity, essentially filtering out most of the slow-wave spectrum. N3 sleep would be nearly impossible to score correctly at this setting.

Exam Trap

Confusing LFF recommendations for different channels: EEG = 0.3 Hz, EMG = 10 Hz, EOG = 0.3 Hz, ECG = 0.3 Hz. The question specifically asks about EEG — answer with the EEG setting, not the EMG setting.

Memory Anchor

EEG LFF = 0.3 Hz (preserves delta 0.5-2 Hz). EMG LFF = 10 Hz. Same question, different channel = different answer.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During PSG, the oronasal thermal sensor shows no airflow during a 30-second period, but the nasal pressure transducer shows a reduced signal and effort belts show continued effort. The MOST likely explanation is:

options.text: The thermal sensor is more sensitive and is detecting a true apnea.
The pressure transducer is picking up cardiac artifact misinterpreted as airflow.
The airflow is of very low amplitude (hypopnea range), and the thermal sensor — which detects temperature change — is less sensitive to low-flow events than the nasal pressure transducer.
The thermal sensor has completely failed.

rationales.whyCorrect:
The oronasal thermal sensor (thermistor or thermocouple) detects airflow by sensing temperature changes between inspired (cooler) and expired (warmer) air. The nasal pressure transducer detects airflow by measuring pressure fluctuations at the nares. These sensors have fundamentally different sensitivity characteristics: the pressure transducer is MORE sensitive to low-amplitude airflow (making it the recommended sensor for hypopnea detection), while the thermal sensor is LESS sensitive to low flows because small-volume breaths produce minimal temperature change. In this scenario, the thermal sensor shows no airflow (suggesting apnea), but the pressure transducer shows reduced signal (suggesting hypopnea) and effort belts show continued effort. This pattern — thermal flatline + pressure signal present + effort present — indicates a low-flow state (hypopnea) that falls below the thermal sensor's detection threshold but is still detected by the more sensitive pressure transducer.

**Clue in the question.** Thermal sensor = no airflow, pressure transducer = reduced signal, effort = present. This discrepancy is explained by the differing sensitivity of the two sensor types, not by sensor failure.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Sensor sensitivity differences — thermal vs. pressure transducer.
rationales.eli10:
The sleep study uses two different ways to measure breathing. The thermal sensor (the little prongs by your nose and mouth) detects the warmth of your breath — it's like feeling someone's breath on your hand. The pressure sensor detects the push of air — it's more sensitive, like a very light wind detector. When breathing becomes very shallow (a hypopnea), the thermal sensor might not feel enough warmth to detect it, but the pressure sensor still picks up the slight air movement. That's why they show different things: the thermal sensor thinks there's no breathing, but the pressure sensor still sees some.

ELI Example

Like two ways to tell if a fan is on: (1) holding your hand in front to feel the breeze (pressure transducer — sensitive, detects even a gentle breeze), vs. (2) checking if the air feels warm (thermal sensor — needs stronger airflow to register a temperature change). A fan on "low" might not feel warm but you can still feel the breeze.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** The thermal sensor is LESS sensitive, not more sensitive — that's why it misses the low-flow signal that the pressure transducer detects. If both sensors agreed on zero flow, that would indicate true apnea.

**B.** Cardiac artifact on the pressure transducer would appear as small, rhythmic oscillations at heart rate, not as a reduced but present respiratory airflow signal. The pressure transducer is showing actual (low) airflow, not artifact.

**D.** A complete thermal sensor failure would produce a flat line constantly (during both inspiration and expiration), not selectively during a 30-second period while the patient continues to show effort and some pressure signal. The pattern is consistent with hypopnea, not sensor failure.

Exam Trap

Assuming that when two sensors disagree, one must be broken. The exam tests whether you understand that thermal and pressure sensors have different sensitivity ranges and that discrepancy between them is EXPECTED during low-flow events.

Memory Anchor

Thermal = apnea sensor (less sensitive, good for confirming absence of airflow). Pressure transducer = hypopnea sensor (more sensitive, detects low flow). Disagreement during low flow = hypopnea, not sensor failure.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: For a standard 4-nap MSLT following a PSG with 7.2 hours of total sleep time, the first nap trial begins:

options.text: 1.5 to 3 hours after the PSG concludes.
Immediately upon awakening.
Exactly 2 hours after lights-on.
At 9:00 AM regardless of PSG awakening time.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Per standardized MSLT protocol, the first nap trial begins 1.5 to 3 hours after the overnight PSG concludes (lights on). This interval allows the patient time for morning hygiene, breakfast, and settling into the daytime testing environment. The preceding PSG must document at least 6 hours of total sleep time (this patient had 7.2 hours — adequate) for the MSLT results to be valid. The nap trials are then conducted at 2-hour intervals, with each trial lasting either 20 minutes (no sleep) or 15 minutes after sleep onset. The specific start time depends on the PSG conclusion time, not a fixed clock time.

**Clue in the question.** "MSLT following a PSG" and "7.2 hours of total sleep time" — the PSG duration is provided to confirm adequacy (≥6 hours), and the 1.5-3 hour interval is the protocol-standard post-PSG wait.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Procedures and Practice Guidelines: MSLT timing protocol.
rationales.eli10:
After a full night of being monitored in the sleep lab, the patient can't just roll out of bed and immediately start the daytime nap test. The rules say there must be a break of at least 1.5 hours (but no more than 3 hours) between when the overnight test ends and when the first nap starts. This gives the patient time to use the bathroom, eat breakfast, and get comfortable for a full day of napping at scheduled times. The overnight test needs to show the patient got at least 6 hours of sleep, which this patient did.

ELI Example

Like a double-feature movie marathon — you don't start the second movie the instant the first one ends. There's an intermission for bathroom, snacks, and stretching. The MSLT has a mandatory "intermission" of 1.5-3 hours between the overnight movie (PSG) and the daytime show (nap trials).

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** Starting immediately upon awakening does not allow the "washout" of sleep inertia and fails to standardize the pre-nap conditions. Sleep inertia could artifactually shorten the first nap latency.

**C.** "Exactly 2 hours" is too rigid. The protocol specifies a range (1.5-3 hours), not a fixed interval. Individual lab schedules and patient needs may require flexibility within that window.

**D.** 9:00 AM regardless of PSG awakening time ignores the patient's actual sleep-wake schedule. If the PSG concludes at 8:00 AM, starting at 9:00 AM would be only 1 hour later — below the 1.5 hour minimum.

Exam Trap

Knowing there's a 2-hour interval between MSLT NAPS (correct) and confusing this with the PSG-to-first-nap interval (1.5-3 hours, also commonly rounded to 2 hours but technically a range). The exam may test the distinction between inter-nap interval (2 hours) and post-PSG interval (1.5-3 hours).

Memory Anchor

First MSLT nap = 1.5-3 hours after PSG ends. Between naps = 2 hours apart. PSG must show ≥6 hours sleep for valid MSLT.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During PSG with CPAP at 10 cm H2O, the PAP flow signal intermittently drops to zero during exhalation. The mask is properly fitted and the patient is asleep. The MOST likely cause is:

options.text: The patient is experiencing central apneas requiring higher pressure.
The high-frequency filter on the flow channel is set too low.
The PAP device is cycling into a pressure relief mode.
The patient is exhaling through the mouth while using a nasal mask, causing loss of exhaled flow signal at the nasal sensor.

rationales.whyCorrect:
During CPAP with a nasal mask, the PAP flow signal is derived from sensors within the CPAP device that measure flow through the circuit — but this flow path assumes the patient breathes entirely through the nose. When a patient opens their mouth during exhalation with a nasal mask, the exhaled air takes the path of least resistance — out through the open mouth — bypassing the nasal mask and the CPAP circuit entirely. This causes the CPAP flow signal to drop to zero during exhalation (no exhaled air passes through the circuit to be measured) while inspiration flow is preserved (the CPAP pressurizes the nasal airway and some inspiratory flow is detected). The mask may remain properly fitted — a nasal mask does not cover the mouth, so it cannot prevent mouth breathing. This pattern is common and does not necessarily indicate a problem requiring intervention unless it causes significant leak or sleep disruption.

**Clue in the question.** "PAP flow signal intermittently drops to zero during EXHALATION" with a nasal mask and "mask is properly fitted" — exhalation-only flow loss with nasal interface = mouth breathing.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: PAP flow signal interpretation — mouth leak.
rationales.eli10:
When a patient wears a CPAP mask that only covers the nose, the machine assumes all air goes in and out through the nose. If the patient's mouth falls open while breathing out, the air takes the easy way — right out the mouth — and the CPAP machine can't "see" that exhaled breath because it bypasses the nasal mask entirely. The machine still shows air going IN (through the nose, pushed by the CPAP pressure), but the exhaled breath going OUT through the mouth reads as zero. It's a common situation and usually not a big problem unless too much air leaks.

ELI Example

Like trying to measure how much water comes out of a garden hose by only watching the nozzle — but the hose has a hidden leak halfway down. Water still comes out the nozzle (inspiration), but some (or all) of the returning water sprays out the leak (mouth exhalation) and never reaches your measurement point.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Central apneas involve absence of BOTH inspiratory and expiratory flow, not just expiratory flow loss. Central apneas also show absent effort; this question describes continued effort. Isolated expiratory flow loss is not a central apnea pattern.

**B.** A high-frequency filter set too low would attenuate rapid signal changes continuously, not produce intermittent zero-flow during exhalation only. Filter issues affect the entire waveform, not just the expiratory phase.

**C.** Pressure relief mode (e.g., C-Flex, EPR) reduces pressure during early exhalation but does not cause the flow signal to drop to zero unless the pressure reduction is extreme enough to allow airway collapse, which would also affect inspiratory flow.

Exam Trap

Assuming any loss of flow signal during CPAP means the patient is having respiratory events. The exam tests whether you can distinguish true apneas (no flow in either direction) from mouth leak (flow loss during exhalation only with nasal interface).

Memory Anchor

Nasal mask + exhalation-only flow loss = mouth breathing/mouth leak. Inspiration preserved = not apnea. Consider chin strap or full-face mask if problematic.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A technologist troubleshoots 60 Hz interference appearing as a uniform sinusoidal pattern on all EEG channels. Which intervention is LEAST likely to reduce this artifact?

options.text: Re-checking all electrode impedances to ensure they are below 5 kOhm and well-matched.
Ensuring lead wires are twisted together and not crossing power cables.
Increasing the high-frequency filter — because 60 Hz is within the EEG bandwidth and the HFF attenuates frequencies above its cutoff, not a narrow 60 Hz band.
Improving the ground electrode connection.

rationales.whyCorrect:
This question asks for the LEAST likely intervention to reduce 60 Hz artifact. The high-frequency filter (HFF, or low-pass filter) attenuates frequencies ABOVE its cutoff. The standard EEG HFF is set at 35 Hz, meaning frequencies above 35 Hz are progressively attenuated. However, the HFF attenuates a broad range of high frequencies — it does NOT specifically target 60 Hz. To reduce 60 Hz from 35 Hz HFF setting, the HFF would need to be lowered below 60 Hz (e.g., to 15-30 Hz), which would also severely attenuate sleep spindles (11-16 Hz), beta activity (15-30 Hz), and muscle artifact (useful for arousal scoring) — unacceptable signal degradation. Moreover, the HFF is not designed for narrow-band noise rejection. The other three options (check impedances, twist leads away from power cables, improve ground) are all appropriate first-line interventions for 60 Hz.

**Clue in the question.** "LEAST likely to reduce" — three options directly address the root cause of 60 Hz interference; one option (HFF) is a poor workaround that damages signal quality without specifically targeting the interference.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Troubleshooting 60 Hz interference — LEAST effective intervention.
rationales.eli10:
When all the brain wave channels show electrical hum, you want to find and fix the source — not just turn down the volume on everything. The high-frequency filter would reduce the hum but also reduce real brain signals (sleep spindles and fast brain activity). It's like dealing with a noisy neighbor by wearing earplugs 24/7 — sure, you don't hear the neighbor, but you also can't hear anything else clearly. Better solutions: make sure the sensor contacts are good, keep wires away from power cords, and check the ground connection.

ELI Example

If your radio has static, the LEAST effective fix is turning down the treble knob — it muffles the music AND the static. The better fixes: adjust the antenna (check impedances), move away from fluorescent lights (reroute leads), or check the power connection (check ground). Same logic applies to EEG 60 Hz interference.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Re-checking impedances IS effective — well-matched, low impedances (\<5 kOhm) maximize common-mode rejection, which is the amplifier's main defense against 60 Hz interference.

**B.** Twisting lead wires and keeping them away from power cables IS effective — this reduces inductive coupling (the mechanism by which 60 Hz enters the signal path).

**D.** Improving the ground electrode connection IS effective — a poor ground increases the impedance to earth, reducing the amplifier's ability to reject common-mode noise.

Exam Trap

Thinking "filter" whenever you see "artifact." The exam tests whether you understand which filter addresses which problem. The HFF is for reducing high-frequency noise broadly, not for targeted 60 Hz removal. A notch filter (not the HFF) is the filter designed for 60 Hz — and even that is discouraged for routine use (see Q024).

Memory Anchor

60 Hz on all channels → check impedances, reroute leads, check ground. HFF is the LEAST effective because it's a blunt instrument that damages signal quality.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A technologist performs biocalibration on a patient with a known seizure disorder. Regarding additional calibration maneuvers:

options.text: Have the patient hold their breath for 30 seconds to assess hypoxic EEG changes.
Perform intermittent photic stimulation only if specifically ordered by the physician.
Ask the patient to hyperventilate for 3 minutes only if specifically ordered and deemed safe.
No additional standard biocalibration maneuvers are needed beyond the standard protocol; additional activation procedures require a specific physician order.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Standard biocalibration maneuvers (eyes open/close, eye movements, jaw clench, breath hold, foot flexion) are designed to verify sensor function and provide baseline signals — they are not activation procedures designed to provoke EEG abnormalities. Activation procedures like hyperventilation and intermittent photic stimulation are specifically designed to provoke epileptiform discharges and are NOT part of the standard PSG biocalibration protocol. Performing activation procedures — especially in a patient with known seizure disorder — without a specific physician order exceeds the technologist's scope of practice and introduces unnecessary risk of inducing a seizure. The standard PSG biocalibration is sufficient for verifying channel function; no additional maneuvers are indicated solely because the patient has a seizure history.

**Clue in the question.** "Patient with a known seizure disorder" and "additional calibration maneuvers" — the question tests whether you know that seizure-specific activation procedures are NOT part of routine biocalibration and require physician orders.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Procedures and Practice Guidelines: Biocalibration in patients with seizure disorders.
rationales.eli10:
The standard setup checks (open/close eyes, look around, clench jaw, etc.) are safe for everyone and just confirm the equipment is working. But special tests designed to trigger seizure activity on purpose — like flashing lights or having the patient breathe fast and deep — are NOT part of routine setup. For a patient who already has seizures, doing these extra tests without a doctor specifically ordering them could trigger a seizure unnecessarily. The standard checks are enough.

ELI Example

Standard biocalibration is like a car's routine safety check — lights, horn, wipers. Activation procedures (hyperventilation, photic stimulation) are like stress-testing the engine on a racetrack — you only do that if the mechanic specifically orders it, especially if the car already has a known engine problem.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Having the patient hold their breath for 30 seconds to assess hypoxic EEG changes is not a standard biocalibration maneuver and could be dangerous. The standard breath-hold during biocalibration is brief and used to verify respiratory channels, not to provoke EEG changes.

**B.** Intermittent photic stimulation (IPS) is an activation procedure, NOT a standard biocalibration maneuver. It requires a specific physician order and is typically performed during extended EEG, not routine PSG.

**C.** Hyperventilation for 3 minutes is an activation procedure that can provoke absence seizures and focal epileptiform discharges. It requires a specific physician order and safety screening. It is NOT a standard PSG biocalibration maneuver.

Exam Trap

Assuming that a patient with a neurological history needs "extra" biocalibration. The exam tests whether you understand the boundary between routine technologist-performed setup (safe, standardized, for equipment verification) and physician-ordered diagnostic procedures (provocative, risk-carrying, for clinical diagnosis).

Memory Anchor

Seizure patient + PSG = standard biocalibration only. Hyperventilation and photic stimulation = activation procedures = require physician order. Don't add provocative maneuvers to routine setup.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During 10-20 lead placement, nasion-to-inion distance is 38 cm. Fpz is located at what distance from the nasion along the midline?

options.text: 10% of the nasion-to-inion distance = 3.8 cm.
20% of the nasion-to-inion distance = 7.6 cm.
10% of the head circumference along the sagittal plane.
The midpoint between nasion and vertex (Cz).

rationales.whyCorrect:
In the International 10-20 system, measurements along the sagittal (midline) plane are made as percentages of the nasion-to-inion distance. Fpz (frontopolar midline) is the first electrode encountered when moving posteriorly from the nasion along the midline, located at 10% of the nasion-to-inion distance above the nasion. Given nasion-to-inion = 38 cm, Fpz = 10% × 38 cm = 3.8 cm. This is one of the fundamental 10-20 measurements that technologists must be able to calculate. The midline electrodes, in order from nasion to inion, are: nasion → Fpz (10%) → Fz (30%) → Cz (50%) → Pz (70%) → Oz (90%) → inion (100%).

**Clue in the question.** "Nasion-to-inion distance is 38 cm" and "Fpz" — Fpz is the first midline electrode at 10% from the nasion.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: 10-20 system — Fpz placement.
rationales.eli10:
Picture a line drawn from the bridge of your nose to the bump at the back of your head. The 10-20 system divides this line into percentage segments. The very first electrode spot (Fpz, at your forehead) is 10% of the way along this line from your nose. With a 38 cm line, that's just under 4 cm up from your nose. It's like a ruler where the nose is at 0% and the back of your head is at 100%.

ELI Example

Imagine a string laid along the top of your head from nose to back — like a measuring tape running over a globe. Mark every 10% of the length. The first mark at 10% is Fpz (forehead). The third mark at 30% is Fz. The middle at 50% is Cz (top of head). The percentages are the electrodes' "addresses" along that line.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** 20% of the nasion-to-inion distance (7.6 cm) locates approximately between Fpz and Fz, not Fpz. Fpz is at 10%.

**C.** The 10-20 system uses percentages of the nasion-to-inion (or preauricular-to-preauricular) distance, NOT percentages of head circumference. Head circumference is not used in electrode placement calculations.

**D.** The midpoint between nasion and vertex is 50% of the nasion-to-inion distance — which is Fz (30% from nasion) or Cz (50% from nasion), not Fpz (10%).

Exam Trap

Confusing the percentage for Fpz (10%) with nearby electrodes like Fz (30%) or thinking Fpz is at 20%. The mnemonic is "Fpz is first" — first electrode from nasion, at the first 10% mark.

Memory Anchor

Midline 10-20 from nasion: Fpz (10%) → Fz (30%) → Cz (50%) → Pz (70%) → Oz (90%). Fpz is FIRST at 10%.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During pre-study equipment check, the headbox produces an electrical tingle when touched. Leakage current measures 150 microamps. The MOST appropriate action is:

options.text: Remove the headbox from service, tag it as faulty, and use a replacement that passes electrical safety testing, because any perceptible leakage current indicates a safety hazard.
Proceed — 150 microamps is within the 500 microamp limit.
Proceed but instruct the patient not to touch the headbox.
Wrap the headbox in electrical tape to insulate it.

rationales.whyCorrect:
A perceptible "electrical tingle" when touching the headbox is NEVER acceptable, regardless of the measured current value. The patient is connected to the headbox via electrodes that provide a low-resistance pathway through the skin — any leakage current that is perceptible to the technologist could be dangerous (or fatal) if it flows through the patient, especially with the reduced skin impedance created by electrode abrasion and conductive paste. The acceptable leakage current limit for medical equipment applied to patients is typically 100 microamps or less (per IEC 60601 standards). A reading of 150 microamps exceeds this limit. Regardless of the number, a perceptible tingle means the insulation has failed and current is flowing where it should not — the device must be immediately removed from service, tagged as faulty, and replaced.

**Clue in the question.** "Electrical tingle when touched" and "leakage current measures 150 microamps" — any perceptible current through a patient-connected device is a safety hazard requiring immediate removal from service.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Electrical safety — leakage current.
rationales.eli10:
If you touch the headbox (the box that all the patient's wires plug into) and feel even a tiny electric tingle, that's a huge red flag. The patient is plugged into this same box with wires that go directly onto their prepped skin — meaning electricity has an even easier path into their body than yours. Even if a meter says the current is "within limits," if you can FEEL it, it's not safe. Unplug it, label it as broken, and get a replacement. Never gamble with electrical safety.

ELI Example

If you touch a toaster and feel a tingle, you unplug it and throw it out — you don't measure the current and decide it's "within limits." The headbox is even more dangerous because the patient is wired directly to it with low-resistance skin contact, making them far more vulnerable to electrical injury than you are touching the outside case.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** 150 microamps is NOT within acceptable limits for patient-applied parts. IEC 60601 limits patient leakage current to 100 microamps under normal conditions. Additionally, the perceptible tingle means the current path involves the chassis, which indicates insulator failure — the measured 150 may not capture the full hazard.

**C.** Instructing the patient not to touch the headbox does not address the hazard — the patient is already connected to the headbox via electrodes, creating a conductive path through their body that is more dangerous than touching the case.

**D.** Wrapping the headbox in electrical tape is an unsafe improvised "repair" that does not address the underlying insulation failure. Electrical tape is not rated for medical device chassis insulation and can degrade, peel, or provide incomplete coverage.

Exam Trap

Trying to interpret the numeric leakage current value instead of focusing on the clinical sign: perceptible tingle = immediate removal. The exam may give you a borderline number to see if you overthink the measurement and ignore the obvious hazard.

Memory Anchor

Perceptible electrical tingle from any patient-connected equipment = remove from service immediately. No exceptions, no measurements needed. Patient safety overrides all other considerations.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: For a pediatric PSG on a 4-month-old infant, which additional monitoring parameter is recommended compared with standard adult PSG?

options.text: Continuous transcutaneous CO2 (TcCO2) or end-tidal CO2 (ETCO2) monitoring, because infants are at higher risk for hypoventilation and CO2 retention.
Invasive arterial blood pressure monitoring.
Continuous core body temperature via esophageal probe.
Four-limb blood pressure monitoring cycling every 5 minutes.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Infants (particularly those under 6 months) have immature respiratory control mechanisms, a highly compliant chest wall, and a higher metabolic rate — all of which increase their risk for hypoventilation and CO2 retention during sleep. Standard pulse oximetry detects oxygen desaturation, which is a LATE finding in hypoventilation — by the time SpO2 drops, significant CO2 retention has already occurred. Continuous CO2 monitoring (either ETCO2 via nasal cannula sampling or TcCO2 via heated skin sensor) provides early detection of hypoventilation by directly measuring CO2 levels. AASM guidelines and pediatric sleep medicine standards specifically recommend CO2 monitoring for infants and young children undergoing PSG. This is the single most important additional monitoring parameter for infant PSG compared to standard adult setup.

**Clue in the question.** "4-month-old infant" and "additional monitoring parameter recommended" — infants have immature respiratory control, making CO2 monitoring essential beyond the standard adult montage.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Pediatric PSG — infant-specific monitoring.
rationales.eli10:
Babies breathe differently than adults — their breathing control system isn't fully developed yet, and they're more likely to have episodes where they don't breathe deeply enough (hypoventilation). A regular oxygen monitor only catches the problem late, after oxygen has already dropped. But a CO2 monitor catches the problem early by detecting when CO2 is building up — like a carbon monoxide detector that warns you before the air becomes dangerous. This extra safety monitoring is essential for babies in the sleep lab.

ELI Example

A pulse oximeter is like a fire alarm — it tells you when things are already bad (oxygen is low). A CO2 monitor is like a smoke detector — it warns you at the earliest sign of trouble (CO2 is rising) before the fire (oxygen desaturation) actually starts.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** Invasive arterial blood pressure monitoring requires arterial catheterization — a procedure performed in an ICU, not a sleep lab. This is far too invasive for routine pediatric PSG.

**C.** Core body temperature via esophageal probe is invasive, carries risk of esophageal perforation, and is not standard for PSG. Temperature is not a primary sleep study variable.

**D.** Four-limb blood pressure monitoring cycling every 5 minutes would severely disrupt sleep with frequent cuff inflations and is not indicated for routine PSG. It might be used in specific research protocols but is not standard.

Exam Trap

Assuming invasive monitoring (arterial lines, esophageal probes) is "better" because it's more direct. The exam tests whether you know the appropriate LEVEL of monitoring for the clinical setting. A sleep lab is not an ICU — monitoring should be effective but non-invasive and sleep-compatible.

Memory Anchor

Infant PSG (\<6 months) = add continuous CO2 monitoring (ETCO2 or TcCO2). Detects hypoventilation earlier than oximetry alone. Not invasive — standard of care for infants.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A technologist sets up PSG for a patient with known latex allergy. The MOST important equipment preparation step is:

options.text: Apply barrier film under all electrodes.
Use only disposable electrodes for all channels.
Verify that all patient-contact supplies — electrodes, tape, belts, tubing, masks — are latex-free and have latex-free alternatives available.
Proceed with standard supplies and treat any reaction with antihistamines if it occurs.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Latex allergy (Type I IgE-mediated hypersensitivity) can cause reactions ranging from contact urticaria to anaphylaxis. Many medical supplies historically contained natural rubber latex, including electrode adhesives, medical tape, elastic belts, and some tubing. For a patient with a known latex allergy, the technologist must proactively verify that ALL supplies that will contact the patient are latex-free BEFORE the study begins. This requires checking product labeling and having documented latex-free alternatives available. Treating a reaction with antihistamines after it occurs (option D) is reactive rather than preventive and fails the standard of care — anaphylaxis cannot always be reversed with antihistamines. Barrier film may reduce but does not eliminate contact risk, and many reactions are airborne (latex proteins can aerosolize on powder from gloves).

**Clue in the question.** "Patient with known latex allergy" and "MOST important equipment preparation step" — the key is PREVENTION through verification, not treatment after exposure.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Latex allergy precautions in PSG.
rationales.eli10:
Some people are severely allergic to latex (natural rubber), which is found in many medical supplies like certain tapes, electrode stickers, elastic bands, and tubing. If a patient tells you they have a latex allergy, you can't just hope for the best — you MUST check every single item that will touch their skin to make sure it's latex-free. A latex reaction can range from a rash to a life-threatening breathing emergency, so this isn't something you manage after it happens — you prevent it entirely.

ELI Example

Like preparing food for someone with a peanut allergy — you don't just cook as usual and keep an EpiPen nearby. You check every ingredient label, avoid cross-contamination, and ensure everything is peanut-free BEFORE you start cooking. Same principle for latex allergy in the sleep lab.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Barrier film under electrodes reduces direct skin contact but does NOT prevent airborne latex protein exposure from powdered latex items, and it does not address other contact points (belts, tubing, masks). It's a partial measure, not comprehensive protection.

**B.** Using disposable electrodes alone does not guarantee latex-free — many disposable electrodes historically contained latex in adhesives. All supplies must be verified latex-free, not just electrodes.

**D.** Proceeding with standard supplies and treating a reaction if it occurs is below the standard of care. Anaphylaxis can be fatal despite treatment, and the technologist may not have emergency medications immediately available. Prevention is mandatory.

Exam Trap

Choosing a partial measure (barrier film, disposable electrodes) instead of the comprehensive approach (verify ALL supplies are latex-free). The exam tests whether you understand that latex allergy requires systematic prevention, not partial barriers.

Memory Anchor

Latex allergy = verify ALL patient-contact supplies are latex-free BEFORE study. Not just electrodes — everything: tape, belts, tubing, masks. Prevention, not treatment.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The recommended sampling rate for the pulse oximeter channel in digital PSG is at least:

options.text: 1 Hz, because oxygen saturation changes slowly.
10 Hz, to capture the pulsatile waveform.
100 Hz, matching the EEG requirement.
25 Hz, to adequately capture the plethysmography waveform for pulse rate and artifact identification.

rationales.whyCorrect:
The pulse oximeter produces two outputs: the SpO2 value and the plethysmographic (pulse) waveform. While the SpO2 value itself changes slowly (over seconds to minutes) and could theoretically be captured at 1 Hz, the plethysmographic waveform contains higher-frequency components (the pulsatile waveform at heart rate, typically 60-100 bpm = 1-1.7 Hz, plus waveform morphology details). To adequately capture the waveform morphology for reliable pulse rate calculation and artifact identification, a minimum sampling rate of 25 Hz is recommended. This provides approximately 15-25 data points per cardiac cycle, sufficient to resolve the waveform shape. At 10 Hz, the waveform is undersampled, losing detail needed to distinguish true pulsations from motion artifact. At 100 Hz, the data is oversampled (excessive file size with no additional clinical benefit).

**Clue in the question.** "Sampling rate for the pulse oximeter channel" — the key distinction is that oximetry is NOT just an SpO2 number; it includes a waveform that requires higher sampling.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Pulse oximeter sampling rate.
rationales.eli10:
The finger oxygen sensor doesn't just give a single oxygen number — it also produces a wavy line (the pulse waveform) that shows each heartbeat. To see the shape of each heartbeat wave clearly, the computer needs to "take a picture" of the signal about 25 times per second. If it only checks once per second, you'd miss all the heartbeat detail and just get the slow-changing oxygen number. Faster than 25 times per second is overkill — it just creates bigger files without giving any more useful information.

ELI Example

Like filming a hummingbird's wings — at 1 frame per second, you see nothing but blurs. At 25 frames per second, you can see the wing motion clearly. At 100 frames per second, you see amazing detail but the file is huge and you can already see everything you need at 25 fps.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** 1 Hz would capture the slow SpO2 trend but would completely miss the plethysmographic waveform, making it impossible to identify artifact, verify pulse rate, or assess signal quality. This would be inadequate for clinical PSG.

**B.** 10 Hz provides only 6-10 samples per cardiac cycle at a heart rate of 60-100 bpm, which is marginal. While better than 1 Hz, it may miss waveform morphology details needed for artifact identification.

**C.** 100 Hz far exceeds what's needed for oximetry. While not harmful to signal quality, this is not the recommended minimum — the question asks for the recommended minimum rate, and 100 Hz is excessive, not minimum.

Exam Trap

Confusing the sampling rate for oximetry (25 Hz) with EEG (200-500 Hz) or ECG (500 Hz). Each channel type has its own recommended sampling rate based on the signal bandwidth. The wider the bandwidth, the higher the required sampling rate.

Memory Anchor

Pulse oximeter sampling rate = 25 Hz minimum (captures pleth waveform). EEG = 200-500 Hz. ECG = 500 Hz. PAP flow = 100 Hz. Each channel has its own rate.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: For referential EEG derivations in standard PSG, the reference electrode is recommended to be placed at:

options.text: The vertex (Cz), equidistant from all other electrodes.
The forehead (Fpz), to minimize eye movement artifact.
The contralateral mastoid (M1 or M2), over the bony prominence behind the ear.
The chin, for stable low-impedance reference.

rationales.whyCorrect:
In standard PSG, referential EEG derivations record the voltage difference between each active scalp electrode and a common reference. The recommended reference sites are the mastoid processes (M1 = left, M2 = right), which are the bony prominences behind each ear. Mastoid references are preferred because: (1) they are relatively electrically neutral (minimal brain-generated activity due to distance from cortex and bone attenuation); (2) they provide stable, low-impedance sites; (3) they are conveniently located near the headbox lead connections; and (4) using contralateral mastoids (e.g., F4-M1, C4-M1, O2-M1) increases the inter-electrode distance, maximizing EEG amplitude. Some labs use linked mastoids or an average reference, but the standard single reference is typically the contralateral mastoid.

**Clue in the question.** "Referential EEG derivations" and "reference electrode" — the mastoid is the standard reference site in PSG, not the vertex, forehead, or chin.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Reference electrode placement for referential EEG.
rationales.eli10:
Every brain wave measurement is a comparison between two points: the "active" electrode on the scalp and the "reference" electrode somewhere else. The reference needs to be in a spot that's electrically quiet — like the bony bump behind the ear (the mastoid). This bone-covered area has very little brain-generated electricity, so any voltage difference measured is almost entirely from the scalp electrode's brain activity. Using the bump behind the OPPOSITE ear from the scalp electrode maximizes the signal because they're far apart.

ELI Example

Like measuring the height of a hill — you need a reference point at sea level. You don't measure from another hilltop (Fpz or Cz, which also have brain activity), you measure from the flattest available ground. The mastoid bone behind the ear is the "sea level" for EEG — electrically quiet and stable.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Cz (vertex) is NOT electrically neutral — it sits directly over the sensorimotor cortex and records significant EEG activity (sleep spindles, K-complexes, vertex sharp waves). Using Cz as a reference would subtract out brain activity from every channel.

**B.** Fpz (forehead) is close to the eyes and picks up EOG artifact and frontal EEG activity. It is not as electrically neutral as the mastoid. While some labs use Fpz as a ground (see Q092), it is not the recommended reference.

**D.** The chin (submental) electrodes record high-amplitude EMG activity — using them as EEG references would inject muscle artifact into every EEG channel. The chin is an active EMG site, not a neutral reference.

Exam Trap

Confusing reference electrode placement (mastoid) with ground electrode placement (often Fpz or forehead). Reference and ground serve different electrical functions and go to different anatomical sites.

Memory Anchor

EEG reference = mastoid (M1, M2), the bony bump behind the ear. Electrically quiet, stable, convenient. Not Cz (active), not Fpz (EOG artifact), not chin (EMG).

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A technologist prepares for a PSG on a patient with suspected REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD). Beyond the standard montage, the MOST important addition is:

options.text: Extended 16-channel EEG to detect epileptiform activity.
Esophageal pressure monitoring for respiratory effort.
Continuous time-synchronized video with audio, plus additional EMG electrodes on the upper extremities to capture dream-enactment behaviors.
Transcutaneous CO2 monitoring for hypoventilation.

rationales.whyCorrect:
REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD) is characterized by the loss of normal REM atonia, allowing patients to physically act out their dreams. Diagnosing RBD requires: (1) PSG evidence of REM sleep without atonia (RSWA) on chin and/or limb EMG channels, and (2) video documentation of dream-enactment behaviors. Standard PSG montage includes chin EMG and bilateral anterior tibialis EMG, but for suspected RBD, additional EMG electrodes on the upper extremities (forearm extensors, biceps) are recommended because dream-enactment behaviors often involve arm movements (punching, grabbing, gesturing). Continuous time-synchronized video with audio is essential to correlate EMG activity with observed behaviors and to capture vocalizations (shouting, talking) that are characteristic of RBD.

**Clue in the question.** "Suspected REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD)" — RBD diagnosis requires both EMG evidence (loss of atonia, often in upper extremities) and video documentation of enacted dreams.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: PSG setup for suspected REM sleep behavior disorder (RBD).
rationales.eli10:
People with RBD physically act out their dreams because the normal "paralysis switch" that keeps you still during dream sleep doesn't work. To diagnose this, the sleep study needs: (1) extra muscle sensors on the arms (since dream-enactment often involves arm movements like punching or grabbing), and (2) video recording with sound throughout the night so the doctor can actually see and hear the patient acting out dreams. Standard leg sensors alone might miss the arm activity that's key to the diagnosis.

ELI Example

Standard PSG for RBD is like a security camera that only watches the front door — you'll miss what's happening at the back. Adding arm EMG and continuous video/audio is like adding more cameras and microphones — now you capture the whole picture, including the arm movements and sleep-talking that are the hallmarks of RBD.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Extended 16-channel EEG is useful for evaluating nocturnal seizures (which can mimic RBD) but is not the MOST important addition for RBD specifically. The core RBD findings are on EMG and video, not EEG. Extended EEG may be added but doesn't replace EMG/video.

**B.** Esophageal pressure monitoring is used for upper airway resistance syndrome (UARS) and subtle respiratory events, not for RBD. It provides no information about muscle atonia or dream-enactment behavior.

**D.** Transcutaneous CO2 monitoring addresses hypoventilation, which is not a primary concern in RBD. RBD is a parasomnia of REM sleep, not a respiratory disorder.

Exam Trap

Confusing RBD workup (needs arm EMG + video) with seizure workup (needs extended EEG) or respiratory workup (needs esophageal pressure/CO2). The exam tests whether you can match the additional monitoring to the specific suspected diagnosis.

Memory Anchor

Suspected RBD = add upper extremity EMG + continuous time-synced video with audio. Key findings: REM without atonia + dream-enactment on video.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Before PSG recording, impedance check shows: ground = 1 kOhm, all EEG = 2-4 kOhm, one EOG = 18 kOhm. The correct interpretation is:

options.text: The elevated EOG impedance is acceptable because EOG signals are high-amplitude.
The study can proceed if gain is increased on the EOG channel.
Only ground impedance matters; individual channel impedances are not clinically significant.

The EOG electrode should be re-prepared and reapplied to achieve impedance below 5 kOhm and within 1-2 kOhm of other electrodes, because mismatched impedances reduce common-mode rejection and increase artifact susceptibility.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Differential amplifiers reject signals that are common to both inputs (common-mode rejection, or CMR). This is how they eliminate 60 Hz interference — 60 Hz appears equally on both the active and reference electrodes, so the amplifier subtracts it out. However, CMR depends on the impedances of the two electrode inputs being well-matched. When one electrode has 18 kOhm and the others have 2-4 kOhm, the impedances are mismatched, converting common-mode signals (like 60 Hz) into differential signals that the amplifier CANNOT reject. The result: that EOG channel will be far more susceptible to 60 Hz and other environmental noise than the matched channels. The 18 kOhm electrode must be re-prepared to bring it within 1-2 kOhm of the others and below 5 kOhm.

**Clue in the question.** Impedances: ground = 1 kOhm, all EEG = 2-4 kOhm, one EOG = 18 kOhm — the outlier EOG electrode compromises that channel's noise rejection through impedance mismatch.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Impedance matching for differential amplifiers.
rationales.eli10:
Think of noise rejection like noise-canceling headphones — they work by comparing what enters the left and right ears and canceling out anything that's the same in both. But this only works if both earpieces hear the noise equally well. If one earpiece is muffled (high impedance = poor signal), the noise-canceling breaks down. In EEG, when one electrode has much higher resistance than its partner, electrical noise that should be canceled out leaks through and becomes visible artifact on that channel.

ELI Example

Like balancing a see-saw — it works perfectly when both sides have equal weight, but if one side is much heavier (higher impedance), the see-saw tilts and can't function properly. The differential amplifier needs balanced inputs (matched impedances) to function correctly.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** EOG signals are relatively high-amplitude (50-200 uV) compared to EEG (10-50 uV), but this does not make high impedance "acceptable." High impedance degrades signal quality through increased thermal noise and reduced CMR regardless of signal amplitude.

**B.** Increasing gain amplifies both signal AND noise equally. It does not address the fundamental problem: high impedance causes the amplifier to lose its noise-rejection capability. The signal-to-noise ratio remains poor.

**C.** Ground impedance IS important (should be low and stable), but individual channel impedances are equally important. Each differential amplifier's CMR depends on its own input impedances, not just the ground.

Exam Trap

Thinking that as long as impedances are "close enough" or below some absolute threshold (e.g., 10 kOhm), they're fine. The exam tests whether you understand impedance MATCHING — one outlier among otherwise good impedances is still a problem because it breaks the common-mode rejection.

Memory Anchor

One outlier impedance (even if still under 10 kOhm) among matched impedances → re-prep. Mismatched impedances = poor CMR = noise. Match within 1-2 kOhm of peers, all under 5 kOhm.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A technologist instructs a patient on self-applying an HSAT device at home. The MOST critical instruction for ensuring a technically adequate recording is:

options.text: "Sleep on your back the entire night."
"Apply sensors as demonstrated, avoid alcohol and non-prescribed sedatives, follow your normal sleep schedule, and reattach any sensor that comes off during the night."
"Take a mild over-the-counter sleep aid to ensure adequate sleep."
"If any sensor is uncomfortable, remove it — the recording only needs a few channels."

rationales.whyCorrect:
When a patient self-administers an HSAT at home, the technologist must provide clear instructions that maximize the likelihood of a technically adequate recording. The critical elements are: (1) apply sensors exactly as demonstrated during the in-person or video instruction session; (2) avoid alcohol (which suppresses respiratory drive and can worsen sleep apnea) and non-prescribed sedatives (which can alter sleep architecture and respiratory control); (3) follow the normal sleep schedule (do not go to bed unusually early or late, as this changes the recording duration); and (4) reattach any sensor that becomes dislodged during the night. Alcohol and sedatives introduce physiological confounds; sensor displacement is the most common cause of HSAT failure. Instructions should be encouraging (the patient should try to get a representative night's sleep) but accurate about what to do if problems arise.

**Clue in the question.** "Self-applying an HSAT device at home" and "MOST critical instruction for ensuring a technically adequate recording" — the answer must combine practical application instructions with guidance on avoiding confounds and handling dislodged sensors.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: HSAT patient instructions for home use.
rationales.eli10:
When you send a sleep test home with a patient, they have to set it up themselves. The most important things to tell them are: put the sensors on exactly the way you showed them, don't drink alcohol or take sleep medicine (because those change how you breathe during sleep), go to bed at your normal time, and if a sensor falls off in the middle of the night, try to put it back on. The \#1 reason home sleep tests fail is that a sensor comes loose and the patient doesn't know to reattach it.

ELI Example

Like giving someone a heart monitor to wear at home — you need to teach them exactly where to place the electrodes, warn them not to shower with it on, tell them to keep living normally, and instruct them what to do if a lead comes unstuck. Clear instructions are the difference between a diagnostic recording and a wasted night.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Mandating supine sleep the entire night is impractical and unnatural. Many patients cannot sleep supine, and forcing a position that prevents sleep defeats the purpose of the test. Position should be natural and documented if possible.

**C.** Recommending over-the-counter sleep aids introduces a pharmacological confound. Sedating antihistamines (e.g., diphenhydramine) can affect sleep architecture and respiratory control. The patient should sleep as naturally as possible.

**D.** Instructing the patient to remove uncomfortable sensors results in missing data channels. A recording with missing channels may be non-diagnostic (e.g., no airflow means no apnea detection). The instruction should be to reattach displaced sensors, not remove them.

Exam Trap

Over-prioritizing one aspect of HSAT success (sleep position, sleep aids) while ignoring sensor displacement — the most common cause of technically inadequate HSAT recordings.

Memory Anchor

HSAT home instructions: apply as taught + no alcohol/sedatives + normal sleep schedule + reattach loose sensors. Sensor displacement = \#1 HSAT failure cause.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During PSG, both RIP effort belt channels suddenly show complete loss of signal while SpO2, ECG, and video confirm the patient is breathing. The FIRST troubleshooting step is:

options.text: Wake the patient and recalibrate the belts.
Terminate the study.
Switch to thermal sensor as the sole respiratory monitor.
Check the RIP belt cable connections to the interface box or headbox, as simultaneous loss of both effort channels suggests a disconnected cable rather than a physiological event.

rationales.whyCorrect:
According to the supplied fictional scenario, the patient's SpO₂ has dropped to 72% and remains there. Sustained desaturation below 80% constitutes a medical emergency in the sleep laboratory. The technologist's first responsibility is patient safety — entering the room, assessing the patient, and following the laboratory's emergency oxygen protocol. Documenting or observing without intervening would jeopardize patient safety.

**Clue in the question.** SpO₂ of 72% that does not recover spontaneously — this is a critical desaturation requiring immediate intervention.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify, Respond, and Document: Emergency response to severe desaturation.
rationales.eli10:
When a patient's oxygen level drops very low and stays there, the technologist must go into the room, check on the patient, and give oxygen. Watching from the control room isn't safe enough. It's like a smoke detector — you check for fire now, not "wait and see."

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Continuing the recording without intervening ignores the immediate safety risk of severe hypoxia.

**B.** Increasing CPAP pressure will not address a desaturation that may have a non-obstructive cause.

**C.** Calling the physician before entering the room delays direct patient assessment.

Exam Trap

Assuming all desaturations can be managed from the control room by adjusting PAP pressure. The technologist must physically assess the patient when SpO₂ drops critically low.

Memory Anchor

SpO₂ below 80% and not recovering = enter the room. Do not manage from the control room.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During a split-night PSG, the diagnostic portion records 2.5 hours of sleep with AHI of 55. The technologist initiates CPAP titration. The MINIMUM adequate titration duration should include:

options.text: At least 1 hour with CPAP applied regardless of sleep.
At least 3 hours of total recording time on CPAP.
Exactly 2 hours, after which the study must end.
Sufficient time to demonstrate control of respiratory events across REM and supine NREM sleep, typically at least 3 hours of sleep on CPAP.

rationales.whyCorrect:
A rhythmic, high-frequency artifact appearing uniformly across all EEG channels at exactly 60 Hz is the classic signature of electrical interference. This artifact is caused by electromagnetic coupling from nearby electrical devices, power cables, or poor grounding. Unlike physiological artifact, it is machine-generated and affects all channels equally. The fix involves checking electrode impedances, ensuring proper grounding, and relocating power cables away from patient leads.

**Clue in the question.** Rhythmic, high-frequency, and uniform across multiple channels — this describes 60 Hz electrical interference.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify, Respond, and Document: Recognizing and troubleshooting electrical artifact.
rationales.eli10:
Electricity from wall outlets hums at 60 cycles per second. When this hum gets into the sleep wires, it makes a fast, steady buzz on the recording. It's not from the patient — it's from the power in the walls. Fixing it means checking that no power cords are touching patient wires and that everything is plugged in right.

ELI Example

Like static on a radio when you drive under power lines — the signal leaks in even though it's not part of the broadcast.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Sweat artifact appears as slow baseline drift (0.5-2 Hz), not rapid 60 Hz oscillation.

**B.** Muscle artifact is irregular, burst-like, and varies across channels — not perfectly rhythmic.

**D.** Pulse artifact follows the cardiac cycle, much slower than 60 Hz.

Exam Trap

Confusing muscle artifact with 60 Hz. Muscle is irregular and varies between channels. 60 Hz is perfectly uniform.

Memory Anchor

Rhythmic + fast + same on all channels = 60 Hz. Check grounding and power cord placement.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During an MSLT, between scheduled nap trials the patient should:

options.text: Be allowed to sleep as needed to prevent excessive sleepiness.
Lie quietly in bed in a darkened room for consistency.
Remain out of bed, be monitored to prevent sleeping between naps, and engage in quiet wakeful activities in a well-lit environment.
Exercise moderately to boost alertness.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Slow, rolling baseline shifts (typically 0.5-2 Hz) appearing primarily in EEG and EOG channels indicate sweat artifact. Perspiration changes the electrochemical properties at the electrode-skin interface, altering impedance and producing low-frequency voltage shifts. This is common when patients become warm under blankets or during deeper sleep stages. The artifact is physiological but not neurological — it originates at the electrode site, not the brain.

**Clue in the question.** Slow, rolling baseline undulations appearing gradually — this is the classic sweat artifact pattern.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify, Respond, and Document: Recognizing sweat artifact.
rationales.eli10:
When a patient sweats under the electrodes, the salt in the sweat changes how electricity flows through the skin. This makes the recording line drift slowly up and down like gentle ocean waves. It's not brain activity — it's just sweat. The fix is cooling the room or improving air flow.

ELI Example

Like how a metal detector acts differently over wet versus dry sand at the beach — moisture changes the electrical connection.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** 60 Hz interference is fast and uniform, not slow rolling waves.

**C.** Electrode popping appears as sudden sharp deflections, not gradual drift.

**D.** Pulse artifact is rhythmic and synchronized with the ECG, not gradual baseline drift.

Exam Trap

Confusing sweat artifact with slow-wave EEG activity. Sweat artifact is typically out of phase between channels and does not have the characteristic 0.5-2 Hz high-amplitude morphology of delta waves.

Memory Anchor

Slow, rolling waves that build gradually = sweat. Cool the room, improve ventilation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During the third nap of a 4-nap MSLT, the patient does not fall asleep within 20 minutes. The technologist should:

options.text: Extend the nap to 30 minutes.
Cancel the remaining nap trial.
Repeat the third nap immediately.
Terminate the trial at 20 minutes, document sleep latency of 20 minutes (no sleep), and proceed with remaining naps.

rationales.whyCorrect:
When a reference electrode fails (high impedance or detachment), all channels that share that reference are affected simultaneously. The artifact appears identical across multiple channels because they all share the same compromised reference point. This is a key distinguishing feature from individual electrode problems, which affect only a single channel. The technologist should check the reference electrode impedance and reapply if necessary.

**Clue in the question.** Identical artifact appearing simultaneously on all channels sharing a common reference — this localizes the problem to the reference electrode.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify, Respond, and Document: Troubleshooting reference electrode problems.
rationales.eli10:
Think of the reference electrode as the "zero point" for all the other electrodes. If it goes bad, every channel that uses it goes bad in the exact same way. It's like if the foundation of a house shifts — all the rooms above it shift together. Fix the reference and all the channels come back.

ELI Example

If one speaker in a stereo system fails, you lose one channel. If the amplifier fails, all speakers go silent. The reference electrode is the amplifier — one failure affects everything.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** Individual electrode problems affect only one channel, not all channels identically.

**C.** 60 Hz interference has a characteristic rapid oscillation pattern, not the same as reference failure artifact.

**D.** Equipment failure would typically affect the entire system differently and may produce a flat line rather than identical artifact.

Exam Trap

Trying to fix individual channels one at a time when the pattern clearly shows a shared reference problem. Always check the reference first when all channels show the same artifact.

Memory Anchor

Same artifact on all channels = check the reference electrode first. One bad channel = check that individual electrode.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: For the Maintenance of Wakefulness Test (MWT), a trial is terminated when:

options.text: The patient opens their eyes.
Exactly 40 minutes have elapsed regardless of sleep.
The patient falls asleep — defined as three consecutive epochs of N1 or one epoch of any other sleep stage — or after 40 minutes if no sleep occurs.
The EEG shows any alpha activity for more than 10 seconds.

rationales.whyCorrect:
A sudden complete loss of signal on a single channel, characterized by a flat line or extremely high-amplitude saturation, typically indicates an electrode disconnection. This could be the electrode detaching from the skin, the lead wire disconnecting from the electrode, or a broken wire. The technologist should enter the room, identify the affected electrode, check the connection, and reattach or replace as needed. Checking impedance confirms the problem but reattachment is the corrective action.

**Clue in the question.** A single channel suddenly goes flat while all other channels remain normal — this localizes the problem to that electrode or its lead wire.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify, Respond, and Document: Troubleshooting electrode signal loss.
rationales.eli10:
If one channel suddenly goes flat while all the others look fine, that one electrode probably came unplugged or fell off. It's like one light bulb burning out in a room — the rest still work. The technologist goes in, finds the loose one, and sticks it back on.

ELI Example

If one guitar string breaks during a concert, you don't stop the whole band — you replace or retune that one string.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Increasing the sensitivity amplifies the flat signal — garbage in, garbage out. You can't fix a disconnected electrode by turning up the gain.

**C.** A system reboot is drastic and unnecessary when only one channel is affected; the problem is local.

**D.** Continuing without the channel sacrifices data quality when a simple fix is available.

Exam Trap

Adjusting amplifier settings from the control room instead of physically checking the electrode connection. A flat line is almost always a physical connection problem.

Memory Anchor

One channel flat, rest fine = check that electrode's physical connection. Don't adjust settings — fix the hardware.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The primary clinical difference between the MSLT and MWT is:

options.text: The MSLT measures the tendency to fall asleep in a sleep-conducive environment (physiological sleepiness), while the MWT measures the ability to remain awake in a soporific environment.
The MSLT uses EEG while the MWT does not.
The MWT requires more nap trials than the MSLT.
There is no meaningful clinical difference.

rationales.whyCorrect:
The MSLT consists of five nap opportunities scheduled at 2-hour intervals. Each nap provides data about sleep latency and REM onset. A single nap with no sleep does not invalidate the test. The technologist should continue all five naps as scheduled. The full dataset — not a single nap — determines the mean sleep latency and the presence or absence of sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs). Stopping early or modifying the protocol compromises the diagnostic validity of the test.

**Clue in the question.** The patient did not sleep during one nap of the five-nap MSLT — the protocol requires completing all five naps regardless of individual nap results.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Procedures and Practice Guidelines: Multiple Sleep Latency Test protocol adherence.
rationales.eli10:
The MSLT is a set of five short nap tests spread across the day. Even if someone doesn't fall asleep for one nap, the other four still give useful information. The technologist follows the schedule for all five, no matter what happens in any single nap.

ELI Example

If you miss one question on a test, you don't walk out — you finish the rest and let the total score tell the story.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Ending the MSLT early discards data from remaining naps and may prevent an accurate diagnosis.

**B.** Extending a single nap beyond the protocol-specified duration invalidates that nap's results.

**D.** Repeating the nap immediately deviates from the standard 2-hour interval between naps required by protocol.

Exam Trap

Assuming a single nap without sleep means the test has "failed" or should be stopped. The MSLT protocol explicitly requires completion of all five naps.

Memory Anchor

MSLT = five naps, always finish all five. Never stop early, never extend, never skip a nap.
