rationales.whyCorrect:
Different PSG channels require different minimum sampling rates based on the frequency content of the signals. Respiratory effort belts and thermistor signals contain relatively slow changes and require lower sampling rates (AASM recommends ≥ 25 Hz). Nasal pressure transducers, which detect airflow limitation and subtle waveform changes, require higher sampling rates (≥ 100 Hz). Setting all channels to the same low sampling rate may be adequate for slow signals but will undersample faster signals, missing clinically important waveform details.

**Clue in the question.** Different channels have different frequency content — sampling rates should be matched to the signal, not applied uniformly.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Digital sampling rate requirements for respiratory channels.
rationales.eli10:
Slow signals like breathing belts don't need to be checked as often by the computer. Fast signals like the nasal pressure sensor (which shows the shape of each breath) need faster checking. It's like taking photos — a slow-moving turtle needs fewer photos per minute than a fast-moving hummingbird.

ELI Example

You need more frames per second to film a race car than to film a flower blooming. Same with sleep signals — fast signals need fast sampling.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Uniform low sampling rates undersample fast signals like nasal pressure, missing flow limitation data.

**B.** Uniform high sampling rates waste storage without improving slow signals — but this is generally acceptable if resources permit.

**C.** Sampling rate cannot be changed after the study is recorded; it must be set before acquisition.

Exam Trap

Setting all channels to the same sampling rate without considering the different frequency requirements of each signal type.

Memory Anchor

Sampling rates: EEG ≥ 200 Hz, EOG ≥ 200 Hz, EMG ≥ 200 Hz, Nasal pressure ≥ 100 Hz, Effort/thermistor ≥ 25 Hz, SpO₂ ≥ 1 Hz. Match rate to signal.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The C3-M2 EEG channel shows significantly different amplitude from C4-M1 despite identical amplifier settings. C3 = 3 kOhm, C4 = 4 kOhm, M1 = 2 kOhm, M2 = 15 kOhm. The MOST likely cause of the amplitude discrepancy is:

options.text: C3 is picking up more brain activity than C4 — a normal variant.
The C3-M2 gain is set higher than C4-M1.
The high impedance of M2 (15 kOhm) is causing signal attenuation on all channels referenced to M2, reducing C3-M2 amplitude compared to C4-M1.
M1 impedance is too low, causing excessive C4-M1 signal.

rationales.whyCorrect:
AASM practice parameters for split-night PSG specify minimum criteria before CPAP titration can begin during a single-night study: the diagnostic portion must demonstrate at least 2 hours of recording time with an AHI ≥ 40 (or AHI ≥ 20 with significant desaturation per some protocols), AND sufficient sleep time with REM sleep documented. If these criteria are met, CPAP can be initiated. If not, the entire night should remain diagnostic. The technologist must verify the signals are adequate for scoring before transitioning to titration.

**Clue in the question.** The technologist is determining whether split-night criteria are met — both sufficient diagnostic time/sleep AND adequate signal quality are required.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Procedures and Practice Guidelines: Split-night PSG protocol criteria.
rationales.eli10:
A split-night study is like a two-act play — first you watch the patient's natural sleep (diagnostic), then if they have enough breathing problems, you start CPAP (titration). But you can't start act two until act one has given you enough information. The technologist checks that there's been enough sleep with good signals before switching to CPAP.

ELI Example

You don't start dessert until you've eaten enough dinner to know what you had. Same with split-night — don't start CPAP until you have enough diagnostic data.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** Initiating CPAP too early reduces diagnostic data and may not meet protocol requirements.

**C.** Starting CPAP at a fixed time regardless of clinical findings is not protocol-compliant.

**D.** Terminating without attempting titration when criteria are met wastes the opportunity for a combined study.

Exam Trap

Starting CPAP prematurely based on brief, severe desaturation without verifying that overall criteria for split-night are met.

Memory Anchor

Split-night criteria: ≥ 2 hrs diagnostic recording, AHI ≥ 40 (or ≥ 20 with significant desat), adequate sleep stages documented. Signals must be scorable.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During a split-night PSG, 2.5 hours of diagnostic recording show AHI of 45 per hour with 20 minutes of REM. The technologist should:

options.text: Continue diagnostic recording for another 30 minutes to reach 3 hours.
Initiate CPAP titration, because AHI exceeds 40 during at least 2 hours of recording, meeting split-night criteria.
Terminate the study and schedule a separate titration.
Wake the patient to confirm willingness to proceed with CPAP.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Pulse oximetry relies on detecting pulsatile blood flow; therefore, the probe must be placed on a well-perfused site. Motion artifact is the most common cause of unreliable SpO₂ readings during PSG. Securing the probe and cable with tape, selecting a site with minimal movement (e.g., taping the cable to the hand or forearm), and verifying a clean plethysmographic waveform all reduce motion artifact. The probe should be snug but not tight — excessive pressure can reduce perfusion and degrade the signal.

**Clue in the question.** Motion artifact is the most common cause of unreliable oximetry during sleep — proper probe placement and cable management minimize this.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Pulse oximeter probe application and motion artifact reduction.
rationales.eli10:
The oxygen finger clip works by shining light through the skin to see blood pulsing. If the patient moves, the light bounces around and gives bad readings. Taping the wire down so it doesn't tug on the clip, and putting the clip on a still finger, keeps the signal clean.

ELI Example

A microphone picking up wind noise because the cord is flapping — tape the cord down, and the recording is clean.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** The wrist has poor optical access for pulse oximetry; peripheral digits are preferred.

**B.** The forehead can be used but is more susceptible to venous pulsation artifact; fingers are the standard site.

**D.** Applying firmly to restrict movement could reduce perfusion and degrade signal quality.

Exam Trap

Placing the oximeter probe and walking away without securing the cable. Cable tug from patient movement is a leading cause of SpO₂ artifact.

Memory Anchor

Oximeter = well-perfused digit + secured cable (tape to hand/forearm) + verify pleth waveform. Motion = enemy of good SpO₂.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: The chin EMG uses three electrodes in a triangular arrangement on the submentalis muscle rather than two. The purpose is:

options.text: To allow bipolar recording with a backup electrode in case one fails.
To triple the signal amplitude for better detection of subtle tone changes.
To provide a bipolar derivation using two electrodes, with the third serving as a ground for the EMG channel.
To satisfy a regulatory requirement with no technical basis.

rationales.whyCorrect:
After the study concludes, the technologist should perform a final signal check to document the quality and completeness of the recording. This includes verifying that all required channels were functional throughout the study, noting any periods of signal loss or artifact, and documenting any deviations from the standard montage. This information is essential for the scoring technologist and interpreting physician to assess data reliability and identify any limitations of the study.

**Clue in the question.** Post-study signal verification is a standard quality assurance step — documenting channel integrity supports accurate scoring and interpretation.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Post-study equipment and signal quality documentation.
rationales.eli10:
After the patient goes home, the technologist does a final check of all the recordings. They note if any sensor stopped working during the night, if there was noise on any channel, or if anything was different from the usual setup. The person scoring the study and the doctor reading it need to know these things.

ELI Example

Before submitting a report, you proofread it. The technologist "proofreads" the recording before sending it for scoring.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Skipping this step may result in the scorer or interpreter being unaware of data quality issues.

**C.** Channel function should be verified at the end of the study; the beginning check alone does not confirm function throughout the night.

**D.** Starting analysis with undocumented signal issues can lead to scoring errors or misinterpretation.

Exam Trap

Assuming that a pre-study signal check guarantees signal quality throughout the night. Post-study verification is a separate and essential quality step.

Memory Anchor

Post-study = verify all channels, document signal quality issues, note montage deviations. This protects the scorer and interpreter from working with bad data.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During PSG, the ECG channel shows a flat line with no discernible QRS complexes, but the patient is clearly breathing and moving on video, and oximeter shows a regular pulse at 72 bpm. The MOST likely cause is:

options.text: The patient is in asystole requiring immediate CPR.
The ECG electrodes have become completely disconnected from the patient or the lead wires are unplugged from the headbox.
The ECG amplifier gain is set too low.
The cardiac electrical axis has shifted, making QRS isoelectric in modified lead II.

rationales.whyCorrect:
The ground electrode serves as the common reference point for the differential amplifier system. When the ground electrode has high impedance or is poorly connected, it can inject noise into all channels simultaneously because every channel references the same faulty ground. The technologist should check the ground electrode impedance and connection. "Floating" (disconnecting and reconnecting) the ground may temporarily resolve the issue, but reapplication with proper skin preparation is the definitive fix.

**Clue in the question.** Diffuse, high-amplitude noise affecting all channels simultaneously — this pattern points to a ground electrode problem.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify, Respond, and Document: Ground electrode troubleshooting.
rationales.eli10:
The ground electrode is like the foundation of a house. If it's bad, every room (every channel) has problems. When ALL the channels go noisy at the same time, check the ground first. It's usually the culprit.

ELI Example

If every light in the house flickers, you check the main circuit breaker, not each individual light bulb. The ground electrode is the main breaker.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** 60 Hz typically affects all channels equally but has a characteristic frequency pattern, not random high-amplitude noise.

**C.** Individual electrode problems affect single channels, not all channels simultaneously.

**D.** Increasing sensitivity amplifies noise along with signal.

Exam Trap

Troubleshooting individual channels one by one when the pattern (all channels affected) clearly indicates a common-mode problem like a faulty ground.

Memory Anchor

All channels noisy together = check the ground electrode first. One channel noisy = check that individual electrode.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: Before PSG, the nasal pressure transducer should be calibrated by:

options.text: Having the patient breathe at known flow rates through a pneumotachograph.
Applying a known pressure signal using a manometer and adjusting transducer output to match.
No calibration is needed — the nasal pressure transducer is a qualitative channel.
Using the thermal sensor to calibrate the pressure transducer by comparing signals.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Infection control is a critical patient safety and technologist safety responsibility. After each study, all reusable equipment that contacted the patient (electrodes, belts, sensors, masks) must be cleaned and disinfected according to the laboratory's protocol and manufacturer recommendations. Single-use items (tape, disposable sensors, paste tubes) are discarded. Proper cleaning prevents cross-contamination between patients and maintains equipment longevity. Documentation of cleaning may be required per facility policy.

**Clue in the question.** Post-study equipment processing — infection control protocols apply to all patient-contact items between studies.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Post-study infection control and equipment processing.
rationales.eli10:
After each patient, everything that touched the patient gets cleaned and disinfected. Reusable items like belts and electrodes get wiped down with germ-killing solution. Disposable items like tape get thrown away. This keeps germs from spreading to the next patient.

ELI Example

A restaurant washes plates between customers. The sleep lab cleans equipment between patients. Same principle — different setting.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Storing equipment without cleaning risks cross-contamination.

**B.** "Wiping down" without specific disinfectant may not adequately eliminate pathogens.

**C.** Soaking electrodes in water alone does not disinfect and may damage the electrodes.

Exam Trap

Underestimating the importance of infection control in the sleep laboratory. Treat all patient-contact surfaces as potentially contaminated.

Memory Anchor

Between patients = clean + disinfect reusable items, dispose of single-use items. Document per protocol. Infection control is non-negotiable.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During PSG, ECG artifact appears on EEG channels as sharp biphasic deflections coinciding with each QRS complex. The intervention MOST likely to reduce this artifact is:

options.text: Increasing the EEG HFF to 15 Hz.
Re-referencing EEG channels to a reference further from the heart and great vessels, or using an averaged reference to minimize the ECG voltage gradient.
Applying a 60 Hz notch filter.
Increasing the EEG LFF to 3 Hz.

rationales.whyCorrect:
When a patient wakes up and performs an unusual behavior (such as eating, as described in the fictional scenario), the technologist should document the event thoroughly without unnecessarily intervening. Key documentation includes the time of occurrence, the sleep stage immediately preceding the behavior, any associated EEG patterns, video correlation, and a description of the behavior. The technologist should ensure patient safety but allow the event to occur naturally for diagnostic purposes. This may represent a NREM parasomnia such as sleep-related eating disorder.

**Clue in the question.** The patient exhibits an unusual behavior after awakening from sleep — thorough documentation of the event is the technologist's primary role.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify, Respond, and Document: Documentation of patient-initiated awakenings and behaviors.
rationales.eli10:
If a patient wakes up and does something unusual (like eating), the technologist writes down everything: when it happened, what sleep stage came before it, and what the patient did. They make sure the patient is safe but don't stop the behavior unless it's dangerous. The video and notes help the doctor figure out what kind of sleep problem this is.

ELI Example

A scientist observing animal behavior takes detailed notes without interfering. The technologist is the scientist, and the parasomnia is the behavior being studied.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Forcibly stopping the patient may cause confusion, agitation, and loss of diagnostic data.

**B.** Terminating the study based on one behavioral event is excessive.

**D.** The technologist documents observations but does not diagnose — that is the physician's role.

Exam Trap

Intervening in parasomnia events instead of documenting them. Unless the patient is in danger, observation and documentation are the correct responses.

Memory Anchor

Unusual sleep behavior = document (time, stage, EEG, video, description) + ensure safety. Don't forcibly stop. Don't diagnose.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A patient's skin is oily and electrode paste is not adhering well. The recommended skin preparation technique is:

options.text: Apply additional electrode paste to overcome the oily barrier.
Use alcohol to degrease the skin, then lightly abrade with a cotton swab or abrasive gel to remove oils and dead skin cells, improving adhesion and conductivity.
Skip skin preparation and rely on electrode paste alone.
Use acetone to thoroughly strip all oils from the skin.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Environmental electrical noise (primarily 60 Hz in North America) can be introduced by devices near the patient or recording equipment. Common sources include cell phone chargers, IV pumps, electric beds, fluorescent lights, and poorly shielded power cables. Before troubleshooting electrodes, the technologist should survey the environment for potential interference sources. Simply relocating a charger or turning off unnecessary equipment can resolve the artifact without any electrode intervention.

**Clue in the question.** The artifact appeared after a change in the patient's environment — this suggests an environmental source rather than an electrode problem.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify, Respond, and Document: Environmental sources of electrical artifact.
rationales.eli10:
Sometimes the buzzing on the recording comes from other electrical devices in the room — phone chargers, lamps, medical machines. Before redoing all the electrodes, the technologist looks around for things that might be causing electrical noise. Often, just unplugging a charger or moving a cord fixes it.

ELI Example

A radio buzzes when it's too close to a microwave. Move the radio, and the buzz goes away. Same with EEG and nearby electronics.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Assuming electrode problems without checking the environment may lead to unnecessary electrode reapplication.

**C.** Grounding issues produce a different pattern; environmental noise is often intermittent and correlates with device activity.

**D.** Increasing the low-frequency filter affects slow-wave activity but doesn't address 60 Hz noise.

Exam Trap

Always blaming electrodes for artifact. Environmental sources are common and easier to fix — check them first.

Memory Anchor

New artifact = check environment first (chargers, lights, equipment near patient). Remove sources before touching electrodes.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During HSAT setup instruction, the patient asks what to do if they need to use the bathroom during the night. The MOST appropriate instruction is:

options.text: "Do not get up — this will invalidate the test."
"You may disconnect the sensors from your body but leave the main unit running, then reconnect when you return to bed. Note the time so it can be correlated with the recording."
"Remove all sensors, turn off the device, and restart from the beginning when you return."
"Keep all sensors attached and take the entire device to the bathroom."

rationales.whyCorrect:
The MSLT protocol specifies exactly 2-hour intervals between the start of each nap trial. This standardized interval controls for circadian and homeostatic sleep drive across the day. Deviating from this interval — even for patient convenience — invalidates the comparison between naps and can skew the mean sleep latency calculation. The technologist should follow the protocol strictly and document any unavoidable deviations with an explanation.

**Clue in the question.** The patient requests a change to the nap schedule — MSLT protocol requires strict adherence to the 2-hour interval.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Procedures and Practice Guidelines: MSLT nap interval protocol adherence.
rationales.eli10:
The nap test schedule is precisely timed — naps start exactly 2 hours apart. This isn't flexible. If the technologist changes the timing, the results won't be reliable. Even if the patient asks for an extra 30 minutes, the answer is no — the schedule is fixed for a reason.

ELI Example

A science experiment requires measurements at exactly 2-hour intervals. If you take one measurement at 2.5 hours, you've broken the experiment. The MSLT is the same.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** Extending the interval introduces uncontrolled variables and invalidates the standardized protocol.

**C.** Shortening the interval increases sleep pressure variability.

**D.** Cancelling a nap because of patient preference is not protocol-compliant.

Exam Trap

Accommodating patient requests at the expense of protocol integrity. The MSLT is a standardized test — deviations invalidate results.

Memory Anchor

MSLT naps = exactly 2 hours apart (from start of each nap). No exceptions for patient convenience. Document any unavoidable deviations.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During biocalibration review, the EOG channels (E1-M2 and E2-M2) show in-phase deflections during horizontal eye movements instead of expected out-of-phase deflections. This suggests:

options.text: The patient has a neurological disorder affecting conjugate eye movements.
The EOG electrodes were placed on the wrong sides or there is a wiring error — correct placement should produce out-of-phase deflections for conjugate horizontal eye movements.
The EOG amplifier is malfunctioning.
This is a normal variant requiring no correction.

rationales.whyCorrect:
During an MSLT nap trial, if the patient does not fall asleep, the trial is terminated after 20 minutes. If the patient falls asleep, the trial continues for 15 minutes after sleep onset to assess for sleep-onset REM periods (SOREMPs). Throughout the trial, the technologist should document any external stimuli (verbal prompts, room entries) that might affect sleep latency. Some protocols use audio recording or event marking to document audibility and technologist interactions. This documentation supports the validity of the sleep latency measurement.

**Clue in the question.** The technologist needs to document interactions during the MSLT nap — this is a required protocol component.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Procedures and Practice Guidelines: MSLT nap termination and documentation.
rationales.eli10:
During the nap test, the technologist keeps track of everything they say or do that might affect the patient's sleep — like reminding them to stay awake or adjusting equipment. These notes help prove that the sleep measurements are real and not influenced by outside distractions.

ELI Example

During a hearing test, the technician documents every sound they play. During the MSLT, the technologist documents every interaction they have with the patient.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Verbal interactions with the patient during the nap can affect sleep latency and must be documented.

**B.** Audio recording or event marking is a standard documentation method; "mental notes" are insufficient.

**C.** Documenting only start and stop times misses potentially significant interactions.

Exam Trap

Assuming only sleep data matters during the MSLT. The technologist's interactions are part of the experimental conditions and must be documented.

Memory Anchor

MSLT documentation = sleep latency + sleep stage + SOREMPs + technologist interactions. All are required.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During CPAP at 12 cm H2O, a large mask leak develops (35 L/min on device display), the flow signal shows flattened inspiratory contour, and snoring returns. The technologist should:

options.text: Decrease CPAP pressure because the leak indicates pressure is too high.
Ignore the leak because SpO2 is stable at 94%.

Address the mask leak by adjusting fit, repositioning headgear, or trying a different mask size/type, because large leaks compromise flow and event detection accuracy and may reduce therapeutic efficacy.
Switch immediately to bilevel PAP.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Slow-wave activity (delta waves) during N3 sleep has a frequency of 0.5-2 Hz. If the low-frequency filter (high-pass filter) is set too high — for example, at 1 Hz or 3 Hz — it will progressively attenuate or eliminate these slow frequencies from the recording. AASM recommends a low-frequency filter setting of 0.3 Hz for EEG channels. If N3 is unexpectedly absent in a patient who should have deep sleep, the technologist should verify the low-frequency filter setting before assuming the patient is not generating slow waves.

**Clue in the question.** The patient shows no N3 sleep despite clinical expectation — a high low-frequency filter setting could be filtering out delta activity.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Low-frequency filter settings and slow-wave detection.
rationales.eli10:
Deep sleep produces big, slow brain waves (0.5-2 wiggles per second). If a computer filter is set to block anything slower than 3 wiggles per second, all the deep sleep waves disappear from the recording. The patient IS in deep sleep, but the filter is hiding it. Check the filter setting.

ELI Example

A camera with a filter that blocks red light makes roses look gray. The roses are still red — the filter is just hiding the color. Same with the EEG filter hiding slow waves.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Absent N3 in an appropriate patient population suggests a technical issue, not necessarily normal variation.

**C.** N3 threshold is 20% SWA, but if the SWA is filtered out, no epoch will meet the threshold regardless of true physiology.

**D.** Sensitivity affects amplitude display; filter settings affect whether the waveform is present in the recording at all.

Exam Trap

Assuming absent slow-wave sleep is always physiological. Always check the low-frequency filter before concluding the patient lacks N3.

Memory Anchor

Missing N3 = check low-frequency filter (should be 0.3 Hz for EEG). Filter too high = delta filtered out. Technical check before physiological conclusion.

options.text: Cz, the vertex of the head.
Any convenient scalp location with low impedance.
Fpz or another midline frontal location on the forehead, with low and stable impedance, providing a common reference point for the differential amplifiers.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Per the supplied fictional scenario, the patient reports chest pain via the intercom. Chest pain is a potential cardiac emergency. The technologist must enter the room, assess the patient, and follow facility emergency protocols — which typically include notifying the supervising clinician, calling emergency services if indicated, and terminating the study. Chest pain should never be dismissed as "heartburn" or anxiety without proper medical evaluation. The technologist's primary duty is patient safety.

**Clue in the question.** The patient reports chest pain — this is a potential emergency requiring immediate patient assessment and protocol activation.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify, Respond, and Document: Emergency response to patient-reported chest pain.
rationales.eli10:
Chest pain during a sleep study is never ignored. The technologist goes to the patient immediately, checks on them, and follows the emergency plan — which usually means stopping the test and getting medical help. It's better to be safe than sorry when someone's heart might be involved.

ELI Example

If a passenger on a plane says they have chest pain, the flight attendants don't continue serving drinks — they respond as a medical emergency. Same in the sleep lab.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Dismissing chest pain without evaluation risks missing a serious cardiac event.

**B.** Continuing the study while a patient may be having a cardiac event is unsafe.

**D.** Documenting without intervening delays necessary emergency response.

Exam Trap

Assuming patient-reported symptoms are benign or anxiety-related without proper evaluation. Always take chest pain seriously.

Memory Anchor

Patient reports chest pain = enter room, assess, follow emergency protocol. Don't dismiss. Don't delay. Safety first.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During PSG, the thermal sensor shows airflow during what appears to be a central apnea on nasal pressure and effort channels. The technologist should:

options.text: Disregard the thermal sensor as less accurate.
Score the event as obstructive apnea because the thermal sensor detects airflow.

Recognize that the thermal sensor may produce a low-amplitude signal from room air convection currents or cardiogenic oscillations that does not represent true ventilation, and rely on the nasal pressure transducer and effort channels for event identification.
Immediately replace the nasal pressure cannula as malfunctioning.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Aliasing occurs when a signal is sampled at less than twice its highest frequency component (Nyquist rate). High-frequency signals above the Nyquist frequency "fold back" and appear as lower-frequency artifacts in the recording. For example, muscle artifact (30-100 Hz) sampled at 50 Hz could appear as a 10-20 Hz rhythm mimicking a sleep spindle. Anti-aliasing filters remove frequencies above half the sampling rate before digitization. Ensuring proper sampling rates and anti-aliasing filter settings prevents this type of artifact.

**Clue in the question.** An unusual rhythmic pattern appears that doesn't match expected physiology — aliasing from undersampling could produce such a pattern.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Anti-aliasing filters and sampling adequacy.
rationales.eli10:
If the computer checks the brain signal too slowly, fast wiggle patterns can "disguise" themselves as slow wiggle patterns on the recording — like a fast-spinning fan blade looking like it's spinning slowly in a video. This is called aliasing. The fix is to make sure the computer checks fast enough (high enough sampling rate) and uses anti-aliasing filters.

ELI Example

In old Western movies, wagon wheels sometimes look like they're spinning backward. That's aliasing — the camera isn't taking pictures fast enough to capture the wheel's real speed. EEG aliasing is the same idea.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** 60 Hz has a characteristic appearance distinct from aliasing.

**C.** Electrode popping is a single-event artifact, not a sustained rhythmic pattern.

**D.** Amplifier malfunction produces different patterns (flat lines, saturation, random noise).

Exam Trap

Not considering aliasing when unusual rhythmic patterns appear. Always verify sampling rate and anti-aliasing filter settings.

Memory Anchor

Unexplained rhythmic artifact = check sampling rate (Nyquist: ≥ 2× highest frequency). Anti-aliasing filters must be engaged. Aliasing = fast signals disguised as slow.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During HSAT pre-test education, the patient asks about having a glass of wine with dinner. The MOST appropriate response is:

options.text: "Alcohol has no effect on sleep apnea."

"Avoid alcohol on the day and evening of the test, as it can suppress respiratory drive, increase upper airway collapsibility, and worsen sleep-disordered breathing, potentially affecting test results."
"One glass of wine is fine, but avoid hard liquor."
"Alcohol will improve sleep quality and test accuracy."

rationales.whyCorrect:
Sleep-onset central apneas are a normal phenomenon caused by the instability of the respiratory control system during the transition from wakefulness to sleep. As the wakefulness drive to breathe diminishes and the sleep-related PaCO₂ set point rises, brief central apneas can occur until respiratory control stabilizes. A single, self-limited central apnea at sleep onset in an otherwise healthy patient is not pathological and requires only documentation. Intervention is warranted only if central apneas become frequent, prolonged, or associated with significant desaturation throughout the night.

**Clue in the question.** A single central apnea occurring at sleep onset — this is a well-recognized normal variant.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify, Respond, and Document: Sleep-onset central apnea as a normal variant.
rationales.eli10:
When you first fall asleep, your brain sometimes "forgets" to tell your body to breathe for a few seconds. This is totally normal — it's just the breathing control system adjusting to sleep mode. One or two of these at the beginning of the night isn't a problem. The technologist just notes it and moves on.

ELI Example

A car engine might sputter for a second when shifting from park to drive, then run smoothly. Sleep-onset central apneas are like that — a brief hiccup during the wake-to-sleep transition.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** A single sleep-onset central apnea does not warrant escalating to the clinician.

**B.** Increasing CPAP for sleep-onset central apnea is not indicated and may worsen central events.

**C.** Terminating the study for a normal finding is excessive.

Exam Trap

Overreacting to sleep-onset central apneas. These are normal and common. Distinguish from sustained central apnea patterns (Cheyne-Stokes, treatment-emergent CSA) that occur throughout the night.

Memory Anchor

Sleep-onset central apnea = normal (respiratory control instability during state transition). Document. Don't intervene for isolated events.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During PSG, the left leg EMG shows continuous high-amplitude, high-frequency activity throughout the recording — during wake and all sleep stages — that does not vary with sleep stage. Right leg EMG is normal. This is MOST consistent with:

options.text: Status epilepticus localized to the left leg.
Severe periodic limb movement disorder with continuous movements.
An electrode or lead wire problem — loose connection, damaged wire, or poor electrode contact — producing continuous high-frequency artifact that mimics EMG activity.
Normal EMG in a patient with restless legs syndrome.

rationales.whyCorrect:
A split-night study is a single-night PSG where the first portion is diagnostic and the second portion (if criteria are met) is CPAP titration. Per AASM practice parameters, CPAP titration may be initiated during the same night if: (1) the AHI is at least 40 (or 20-40 with significant desaturation per some protocols) during a minimum of 2 hours of diagnostic recording, and (2) at least some REM sleep has been documented. If criteria are not met, the entire night remains diagnostic, and a separate titration study is scheduled.

**Clue in the question.** The definition of a split-night study — it combines diagnostic and titration portions in one night, contingent on meeting specific criteria.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Procedures and Practice Guidelines: Split-night PSG definition and criteria.
rationales.eli10:
A split-night study is a "two-in-one" sleep test. The first part watches natural sleep to measure breathing problems. If the problems are bad enough and there's been enough sleep, the second part starts CPAP to find the right pressure. If the problems aren't bad enough yet, the whole night stays as just watching — and the patient comes back another night for CPAP.

ELI Example

It's like a two-part exam — you can only move to part two if you score high enough on part one. Otherwise, you take part two on a different day.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Split-night studies do not require two separate nights — that's the point of the combined approach.

**B.** CPAP is not always initiated; it's conditional on meeting diagnostic criteria.

**D.** Any patient with suspected OSA may be a candidate; split-night is not limited to those already diagnosed.

Exam Trap

Thinking a split-night study always includes CPAP. It only includes CPAP if the diagnostic criteria are met. Otherwise, it's just a diagnostic study.

Memory Anchor

Split-night = diagnostic + possible titration, same night. Requires AHI ≥ 40 (or ≥ 20 + desat) and ≥ 2 hrs diagnostic sleep with REM. If criteria not met = diagnostic only.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Per the fictional scenario, the patient exhibits vocalizations during sleep. This could represent a parasomnia (sleep talking, REM sleep behavior disorder) or be associated with seizure activity or respiratory events. The technologist should document the event thoroughly — timing, sleep stage, associated EEG changes, any cardiorespiratory correlates, and video confirmation. The technologist should not intervene unless the patient is in danger. The interpreting physician correlates these findings with the clinical history and other PSG data.

**Clue in the question.** The patient vocalizes during sleep — the technologist documents the event comprehensively for physician interpretation.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify, Respond, and Document: Documentation of abnormal sleep-related vocalizations.
rationales.eli10:
If a patient talks, shouts, or makes sounds during sleep, the technologist writes down everything they observe: when it happened, what sleep stage the patient was in, and what the brain waves and breathing looked like at that moment. The video captures it. The doctor uses all this information to figure out what kind of sleep problem it is.

ELI Example

A court reporter transcribes everything that's said, word for word, without interpreting. The technologist is the court reporter of the sleep study — document, don't diagnose.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** Waking the patient terminates the observable event and loses diagnostic data.

**C.** Vocalizations may be clinically significant; ignoring them discards valuable information.

**D.** The technologist documents observations; the physician makes the diagnosis.

Exam Trap

Either ignoring sleep vocalizations as "just sleep talking" OR overreacting by waking the patient. Document thoroughly and let the physician interpret.

Memory Anchor

Abnormal sleep behavior/vocalization = document (time, stage, EEG, video, cardiorespiratory correlation). Don't intervene unless safety concern. Physician interprets.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During PAP titration, the delivered pressure drops 2-3 cm H2O during each inspiration, returning to set pressure during exhalation. This pattern is MOST consistent with:

options.text: PAP device malfunction requiring replacement.
A normal finding — some inspiratory pressure drop is expected, especially at higher flow demands, as the device compensates for the patient's inspiratory effort.
A large mask leak preventing pressure maintenance.
A circuit obstruction limiting airflow.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Standard EOG placement uses out-of-phase deflections to detect conjugate eye movements: E1 (below left outer canthus) and E2 (above right outer canthus) are referenced to the same electrode (typically M1 or M2). When the eyes move laterally, the cornea (positive) moves toward one electrode and away from the other, producing deflections in opposite directions. If one EOG electrode's wires are reversed, both channels deflect in the same direction during eye movements — a pattern that can be mistaken for artifact or abnormal eye movements. The technologist should verify polarity during biocalibration by having the patient look left and right.

**Clue in the question.** EOG deflections appear in phase rather than out of phase during lateral eye movements — this suggests reversed polarity on one channel.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify, Respond, and Document: EOG electrode polarity verification.
rationales.eli10:
When you look to the right, one eye channel should go up and the other should go down — they move in opposite directions. If both go up together, one of the wires is probably plugged in backward. This is easy to check by having the patient look left and right during setup.

ELI Example

Two dancers doing the mirror image — when one moves left, the other moves right. If both move the same way, someone's facing the wrong direction. Same with EOG channels.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** The eyes themselves are not the problem — the electrode wiring is.

**C.** Sensitivity adjusts amplitude, not the direction of deflection.

**D.** Accepting reversed polarity may cause the scorer to misinterpret eye movements throughout the study.

Exam Trap

Accepting EOG signals without verifying polarity during biocalibration. Always include "look left, look right" in biocalibration to verify out-of-phase deflections.

Memory Anchor

Look L/R during biocalibration = EOG out-of-phase deflections. In-phase deflection = polarity reversed on one channel. Fix wiring.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: During posttest procedures, a patient with diabetes has blood glucose of 58 mg/dL and is shaky and diaphoretic. The technologist should:

options.text: Discharge the patient to eat breakfast at home.
Document the finding and allow the patient to leave.
Follow the laboratory hypoglycemia protocol — typically providing a fast-acting carbohydrate source, monitoring response, and notifying the supervising clinician if the condition does not improve.
Administer the patient's insulin.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Sinus bradycardia during sleep is defined by AASM as a sustained heart rate below 40 bpm for adults. However, in well-conditioned athletes, resting heart rates during sleep in the 30s can be normal due to increased vagal tone. The technologist should recognize that context matters — an athlete with a HR of 38 bpm during N3 sleep without any other concerning findings (no prolonged asystole, no associated desaturation) does not require intervention. Documentation for the interpreting physician is appropriate.

**Clue in the question.** The patient is an athlete with a heart rate slightly below 40 bpm during deep sleep but no other abnormalities — this is likely a normal variant.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Identify, Respond, and Document: Sleep-related bradycardia as a normal variant.
rationales.eli10:
Athletes often have very low heart rates, especially during deep sleep. A heart rate just below 40 in a healthy athlete who's breathing normally isn't dangerous — it's actually a sign of good fitness. The technologist notes it but doesn't worry unless there are other warning signs.

ELI Example

A marathon runner's resting pulse might be 35-40. That's their normal. The sleep study heart rate just reflects their trained heart doing its thing.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** The AASM bradycardia threshold (\< 40 bpm) is a guideline; clinical context (athlete status) must be considered.

**B.** A single borderline-low HR reading in an athlete without other findings does not warrant study termination.

**C.** Escalation is appropriate for sustained bradycardia with clinical compromise, not for an isolated finding in a well-conditioned athlete.

Exam Trap

Applying the bradycardia scoring threshold (\< 40 bpm) rigidly without considering patient context. Clinical judgment matters — a 38 bpm HR during N3 in an athlete is not the same as in a cardiac patient.

Memory Anchor

Athlete + HR just below 40 during N3 + no other findings = document. Bradycardia scoring threshold (\< 40) is a guideline, not an automatic emergency.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: For PSG data acquisition, the ECG channel sampling rate should be set to at least:

options.text: 100 Hz, matching EEG.
200 Hz, for adequate QRS morphology and heart rate variability analysis.
500 Hz, the recommended rate for diagnostic-quality ECG that preserves high-frequency QRS components.
50 Hz, because cardiac signal bandwidth is narrow.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Different PAP modalities serve different clinical needs. CPAP delivers a single continuous pressure and is first-line for uncomplicated OSA. Bilevel PAP without a backup rate (spontaneous mode) provides separate inspiratory and expiratory pressures but requires the patient to initiate all breaths. Bilevel PAP with a backup rate (spontaneous/timed or timed mode) provides mandatory breaths during periods of apnea, making it appropriate for central sleep apnea, hypoventilation syndromes, and neuromuscular disease. The technologist should understand which modality matches which clinical indication.

**Clue in the question.** The patient has central sleep apnea — bilevel PAP with a backup rate is the appropriate modality.

Domain 2: Sleep Study Preparation and Performance — Technical Preparation: Matching PAP modality to patient condition.
rationales.eli10:
There are different types of breathing machines for sleep. Regular CPAP gives one steady pressure. Bilevel gives two pressures — higher when breathing in, lower when breathing out. If the patient sometimes forgets to breathe (central apnea), the machine needs a "backup rate" — it starts the breath for them. The technologist picks the right machine type for the patient's specific breathing problem.

ELI Example

CPAP = cruise control (steady speed). Bilevel = automatic transmission (shifts between two modes). Bilevel with backup rate = self-driving car (takes over when the driver stops).

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** CPAP alone does not address central apneas and may worsen them.

**B.** Bilevel without backup rate cannot address central apneas because it only responds to patient effort.

**D.** While oxygen may be added, it does not address the absent respiratory effort in central apnea.

Exam Trap

Thinking all PAP is the same. The technologist must understand the clinical differences between CPAP, bilevel S, and bilevel S/T modes.

Memory Anchor

CPAP = obstructive events. Bilevel S = obstructive + pressure intolerance. Bilevel S/T = central apnea + hypoventilation (backup rate breaths for the patient).

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A 45-year-old patient's polysomnogram epoch shows the following: alpha rhythm (8-13 Hz) occupies approximately 60% of the epoch over the occipital derivations, rapid eye movements and eye blinks are present on the EOG channels, and the chin EMG demonstrates relatively high tonic activity.

Which sleep stage should be scored for this epoch?

options.text: Stage N1
Stage N2
Stage REM
Stage W (Wake)

rationales.whyCorrect:
Alpha \>50% over occipital with rapid eye movements, eye blinks, and high chin EMG meets all AASM criteria for stage W. Alpha \>50% is the hallmark EEG finding for wakefulness. Together these form the classic triad for scoring W.

**Clue in the question.** Alpha activity \>50% of the epoch is the definitive EEG marker for wake in adults.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Adult sleep stage scoring (Wake)
rationales.eli10:
When awake with eyes closed, your brain produces alpha (8-13 Hz). If alpha fills more than half of a 30-second window and your chin muscle stays tight with eye blinks present, the technologist scores Wake.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Stage N1 shows LAMF activity (mostly theta) replacing alpha, with lower chin EMG, not higher.

**B.** Stage N2 requires sleep spindles and/or K-complexes on LAMF background, not dominant alpha.

**C.** Stage REM requires LOW chin EMG (typically the lowest of the recording), not high tonic activity, and alpha is not characteristic.

Exam Trap

Do not confuse rapid eye movements with REM sleep. Rapid eye movements with HIGH chin EMG and alpha EEG indicate Wake, not REM. REM requires low chin EMG and LAMF EEG without dominant alpha.

Memory Anchor

Alpha \>50% + eye blinks/REMs + high chin EMG = Wake.

Rule Applied

AASM: Score W when alpha rhythm \>50% of epoch over occipital region, OR when eye blinks, reading eye movements, or irregular conjugate REMs with normal/high chin EMG are present.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
During a diagnostic PSG, a 30-second epoch shows low-amplitude, mixed-frequency (LAMF) activity in the 4-7 Hz range replacing the previously observed alpha rhythm. The EOG channels reveal slow, rolling eye movements, and the chin EMG is lower than during wake but not at the lowest level of the recording. There are no sleep spindles, K-complexes, or sawtooth waves.

Which sleep stage should be scored?

options.text: Stage N1
Stage N2
Stage N3
Stage REM

rationales.whyCorrect:
All classic N1 features: LAMF activity in 4-7 Hz (theta) replacing wake alpha; slow, rolling eye movements characteristic of wake-to-N1 transition; chin EMG lower than wake but not at REM atonia. Critically, no sleep spindles, K-complexes, or sawtooth waves confirms N1.

**Clue in the question.** Slow, rolling eye movements with LAMF EEG and no definitive N2 or REM markers = N1.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Adult sleep stage scoring (N1)
rationales.eli10:
When you start dozing off, brain waves slow from alpha to a jumbled mix (mostly theta). Eyes make slow, lazy rolling movements. Chin muscles relax somewhat. No spindles, K-complexes, or sawtooth waves. This is N1.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** Stage N2 requires sleep spindles and/or K-complexes, neither present.

**C.** Stage N3 requires SWA (0.5-2 Hz, \>75 uV) \>=20% of epoch, not present.

**D.** Stage REM requires rapid (not slow rolling) eye movements, sawtooth waves, and lowest chin EMG.

Exam Trap

Do not confuse slow, rolling eye movements (N1) with the conjugate, irregular, sharply peaked eye movements of REM. The type of eye movement is the key discriminator.

Memory Anchor

Slow, rolling eye movements = N1 (transitional sleep). Rapid, jerky eye movements + lowest chin EMG = REM.

Rule Applied

AASM: Score N1 when alpha replaced by LAMF \>50% of epoch. Slow eye movements often present but not required.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A technologist is reviewing an epoch that shows low-amplitude, mixed-frequency EEG background with one clearly identifiable sleep spindle (11-16 Hz, 0.5-2 sec duration) and one K-complex. There is no slow wave activity meeting amplitude criteria. The chin EMG is moderately reduced.

Which stage should this epoch be scored as?

options.text: Stage N1
Stage N2
Stage N3
Stage REM

rationales.whyCorrect:
Under AASM rules, even a single clearly identifiable sleep spindle or K-complex in an epoch with LAMF EEG is sufficient to score N2, provided the epoch lacks enough SWA for N3. One sleep spindle and one K-complex are present with no SWA described.

**Clue in the question.** One clearly identifiable sleep spindle and one K-complex — either alone is enough to score N2.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Adult sleep stage scoring (N2 identification)
rationales.eli10:
Sleep spindles are brief bursts of fast waves (11-16 Hz, 0.5-2 sec). K-complexes are tall, sharp waves. When a technologist sees even ONE of either in a 30-second window with LAMF background, they score N2. It only takes one.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Stage N1 lacks sleep spindles and K-complexes by definition.

**C.** Stage N3 requires SWA \>=20% of epoch; none described.

**D.** Stage REM requires rapid eye movements and lowest chin EMG, neither described.

Exam Trap

A single sleep spindle or K-complex is enough to score N2. Do not wait for multiple spindles or both markers together.

Memory Anchor

One spindle or one K-complex + no slow waves = N2. It only takes one.

Rule Applied

AASM: Score N2 when K-complex(es) and/or sleep spindle(s) present during LAMF EEG, SWA \<20%.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
An epoch on a diagnostic PSG demonstrates a K-complex immediately followed by a sleep spindle on a low-amplitude, mixed-frequency EEG background. No eye movements are present, and the chin EMG is relatively low. There is no slow wave activity and no REM features.

Which sleep stage is this epoch?

options.text: Stage N1
Stage N2
Stage N3
Stage REM

rationales.whyCorrect:
The epoch contains a K-complex immediately followed by a sleep spindle — a classic N2 EEG pairing. Under AASM rules, presence of a K-complex or spindle in an epoch with LAMF background is definitive for N2. No eye movements, relatively low chin EMG are consistent. No SWA and no REM features exist.

**Clue in the question.** A K-complex followed immediately by a sleep spindle is the hallmark N2 finding; either individually confirms N2.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Adult sleep stage scoring (N2 with K-complex-spindle pairing)
rationales.eli10:
A K-complex and spindle arriving back-to-back is a very reliable N2 sign. The K-complex is brief and sharp-looking; the spindle is a tiny cluster of fast waves right after. Together or separately: N2.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** N1 has no spindles or K-complexes; their presence rules it out.

**C.** N3 requires SWA \>=20%; absent here.

**D.** REM never features K-complexes or spindles; their presence definitively excludes REM.

Exam Trap

Never score REM if a K-complex or spindle is present. These waveforms never appear in REM.

Memory Anchor

K-complex + spindle = N2. No exceptions. These waveforms never appear in REM.

Rule Applied

AASM: Score N2 when K-complex(es) and/or spindle(s) present with LAMF EEG, SWA \<20%.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A technologist is scoring an epoch that contains slow wave activity (0.5-2 Hz, \>75 uV peak-to-peak) occupying 22% of the 30-second epoch. A single sleep spindle is also present in the epoch.

What stage should this epoch be scored as?

options.text: Stage N1
Stage N2
Stage N3
Stage REM

rationales.whyCorrect:
AASM defines N3 as epochs with SWA (0.5-2 Hz, \>75 uV peak-to-peak) occupying \>=20% of the epoch. SWA occupies 22%, exceeding the threshold. The sleep spindle is irrelevant once the N3 criterion is met. N3 supersedes N2 in the scoring hierarchy.

**Clue in the question.** 22% SWA exceeds the 20% N3 threshold; the sleep spindle is irrelevant once N3 criteria are met.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Adult sleep stage scoring (N3 threshold)
rationales.eli10:
N3 is deep sleep. If big slow waves fill 20%+ of a 30-second window, it's N3. Here slow waves cover 22% — over the line. The spindle doesn't matter; slow waves are the boss.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** N1 has no SWA and no spindles; neither applies.

**B.** N2 is superseded when SWA \>=20%; N3 takes priority.

**D.** REM lacks high-voltage slow waves.

Exam Trap

Never score N2 when SWA \>=20%, even if spindles/K-complexes are present. N3 takes priority.

Memory Anchor

SWA \>=20% = N3. Spindles and K-complexes don't matter when slow waves dominate.

Rule Applied

AASM: Score N3 when \>=20% of epoch is SWA, regardless of other waveforms.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
An epoch on a diagnostic PSG shows slow wave activity occupying 18% of the 30-second window. A well-formed K-complex is also present. The EEG background is otherwise low-amplitude, mixed-frequency.

How should this epoch be scored?

options.text: Stage N1
Stage N2
Stage N3
Stage REM

rationales.whyCorrect:
SWA occupies only 18%, falling short of the 20% N3 threshold. Since N3 is not met, the presence of a well-formed K-complex makes this epoch N2. Cannot be N3 (SWA\<20%), N1 (K-complex present), or REM (K-complex excludes REM).

**Clue in the question.** 18% SWA is BELOW the 20% N3 threshold; the K-complex then makes it N2.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Adult sleep stage scoring (N2 vs N3 threshold)
rationales.eli10:
20% is the finish line for deep sleep. 18% doesn't cross it. So check what else is there: a K-complex. K-complex without enough slow waves = N2.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** N1 does not have K-complexes; their presence rules out N1.

**C.** N3 requires SWA \>=20%; 18% does not meet the threshold.

**D.** REM does not feature K-complexes; a K-complex in the epoch excludes REM.

Exam Trap

Students see slow waves and jump to N3 without checking the 20% threshold. Always calculate the percentage first.

Memory Anchor

SWA \<20% + K-complex/spindle = N2. SWA \>=20% = N3 regardless of spindles/K-complexes.

Rule Applied

AASM: Score N3 when SWA \>=20%. Score N2 when SWA \<20% but K-complexes/spindles present.

A technologist evaluates an epoch where slow wave activity (0.5-2 Hz, \>75 uV) occupies 45% of the 30-second window. The chin EMG is low, and no sleep spindles or K-complexes are observed.

Which sleep stage should be scored?

options.text: Stage N1
Stage N2
Stage N3
Stage REM

rationales.whyCorrect:
SWA occupies 45% — more than double the 20% N3 threshold. This is unequivocal N3. Low chin EMG is typical for N3. Absence of spindles or K-complexes is irrelevant; N3 does not require them for identification.

**Clue in the question.** 45% SWA massively exceeds the 20% N3 threshold — this is clearly N3.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Adult sleep stage scoring (unequivocal N3)
rationales.eli10:
When almost half the window is big slow waves, you're in deep sleep. 20% is the minimum; 45% is way over. No spindles or K-complexes needed — they're N2 features, not required for deep sleep.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** N1 shows LAMF without slow waves; 45% SWA makes N1 impossible.

**B.** N2 is superseded by N3 once SWA exceeds 20%.

**D.** REM does not contain slow wave activity of this magnitude; high-voltage slow waves exclude REM.

Exam Trap

Don't second-guess N3 because spindles/K-complexes are absent. They are NOT required for N3. The 20% rule stands alone.

Memory Anchor

SWA \>=20% = N3. No spindles needed. No K-complexes needed. Just count the slow waves.

Rule Applied

AASM: Score N3 when \>=20% of epoch is SWA, irrespective of presence or absence of K-complexes or sleep spindles.

What sleep stage is this?

options.text: Stage N1
Stage N2
Stage N3
Stage REM

rationales.whyCorrect:
SWA occupies 35% of this epoch, exceeding the 20% N3 threshold. Under AASM scoring hierarchy, when the N3 threshold is met, the epoch is scored as N3 — the presence of a K-complex does not alter this. N3 is the deepest NREM stage, and once the SWA criterion is satisfied, N3 is scored regardless of coexisting N2 markers.

**Clue in the question.** 35% SWA beats the 20% N3 threshold; the K-complex cannot pull the epoch back to N2.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Adult sleep stage scoring (N3 supersedes N2)
rationales.eli10:
The scoring rules are hierarchical: N3 beats N2, and N2 beats N1. The deepest stage wins. Since slow waves fill 35% (way over 20%), the window gets scored as N3. The K-complex is just along for the ride.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** N1 would lack both SWA and K-complexes; neither is absent.

**B.** N2 is incorrect because SWA threshold for N3 is exceeded; N3 takes priority.

**D.** REM does not contain high-amplitude slow waves; their presence excludes REM.

Exam Trap

Do not score N2 when SWA exceeds 20% just because a K-complex or spindle is present. N3 always supersedes N2.

Memory Anchor

N3 \> N2 \> N1 in the scoring hierarchy. If SWA \>=20%, N3 wins — no matter what else is in the epoch.

Rule Applied

AASM: When SWA \>=20% of epoch, score N3. K-complexes/spindles do not affect N3 scoring.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A 30-second epoch shows low-amplitude, mixed-frequency EEG with distinct sawtooth waves, conjugate irregular sharply peaked rapid eye movements on the EOG channels, and chin EMG at the lowest level observed in the entire recording.

What is the correct sleep stage?

options.text: Stage N1
Stage N2
Stage N3
Stage REM

rationales.whyCorrect:
This epoch contains the classic REM triad: (1) LAMF EEG with sawtooth waves, (2) conjugate, irregular, sharply peaked rapid eye movements on EOG, and (3) chin EMG at the lowest level of the entire recording. Sawtooth waves are a distinctive EEG pattern that often immediately precedes bursts of rapid eye movements and confirm REM sleep.

**Clue in the question.** Sawtooth waves + rapid eye movements + chin EMG at the lowest level of the entire recording = REM.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Adult sleep stage scoring (REM identification)
rationales.eli10:
REM is the dreaming stage. Brain waves look like wake (low-voltage, mixed frequencies) but with a special sawtooth pattern. Eyes dart rapidly. Chin muscle goes almost completely slack — the slackest all night. This combination is REM.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** N1 shows slow, rolling eye movements (not rapid, sharply peaked) and higher chin EMG.

**B.** N2 would have K-complexes or sleep spindles, not sawtooth waves.

**C.** N3 shows high-amplitude slow waves, the opposite of the described low-voltage EEG.

Exam Trap

Do not confuse the LAMF EEG of REM with that of N1. The type of eye movements (rapid vs slow rolling) and chin EMG level (lowest vs somewhat reduced) are key discriminators.

Memory Anchor

Sawtooth waves + REMs + lowest chin EMG = REM. The phrase 'lowest EMG of the recording' only appears in REM scoring rules.

Rule Applied

AASM: Score REM when ALL present: (a) LAMF EEG, (b) low chin EMG (no higher than any other stage, usually lowest), (c) rapid eye movements.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
While scoring a PSG, a technologist encounters an epoch with low chin EMG and conjugate rapid eye movements. However, a clearly identifiable K-complex is also visible within the same 30-second epoch.

What stage should this epoch be scored as?

options.text: Stage N1
Stage N2
Stage N3
Stage REM

rationales.whyCorrect:
Under AASM rules, a clearly identifiable K-complex is definitive for N2, even when the epoch otherwise meets REM criteria (low chin EMG, rapid eye movements). The scoring manual explicitly states: if an epoch contains a K-complex or sleep spindle, score N2 regardless of REMs and low chin EMG. These are NREM-specific waveforms that never occur in true REM.

**Clue in the question.** A K-complex is visible in an otherwise REM-appearing epoch — K-complexes ALWAYS take precedence over REM features.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Adult sleep stage scoring (K-complex in REM-like epoch)
rationales.eli10:
K-complexes and sleep spindles are trump cards. Even if everything else looks like REM — slack chin, darting eyes — if a K-complex is present, the window MUST be N2. K-complexes simply do not happen during real REM sleep.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** N1 has no sleep spindles or K-complexes; a K-complex tells you the patient reached at least N2.

**C.** N3 requires \>=20% SWA, not present (LAMF described).

**D.** REM is incorrect because a K-complex excludes REM per AASM rules.

Exam Trap

Do not be seduced by low chin EMG and REMs into scoring REM when a K-complex or spindle is present. The trump card always wins.

Memory Anchor

K-complex or spindle in any epoch = N2. Full stop. Doesn't matter what the eyes or chin are doing.

Rule Applied

AASM: An epoch containing a K-complex or sleep spindle is scored N2, even if REMs and low chin EMG are present.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A single 30-second epoch contains features of two different sleep stages. For the first 20 seconds, the EEG shows low-amplitude, mixed-frequency activity with slow, rolling eye movements. At approximately 20 seconds into the epoch, a sleep spindle appears and continues for the remainder of the epoch.

How should this entire 30-second epoch be scored under AASM rules?

options.text: Stage N1 for the entire epoch
Stage N2 for the entire epoch
Stage N1 for the first 20 seconds and N2 for the last 10 seconds
Wake for the entire epoch

rationales.whyCorrect:
The AASM transition rule states that when a single epoch contains features of more than one stage, score as the stage occupying the greatest portion. The epoch begins with LAMF EEG and slow eye movements (N1). A spindle appears at ~20 seconds. N1 occupies ~20 sec, N2 ~10 sec. N1 is the majority.

**Clue in the question.** The spindle appears 20 seconds into the 30-second epoch — N1 occupies more of the epoch (20 sec) than N2 (10 sec).

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Adult sleep stage scoring (epoch with multiple stages)
rationales.eli10:
When a 30-second window contains a mix of two stages, score the whole window as whichever stage takes more time. First 20 sec look like N1; last 10 sec have a spindle (N2). 20 \> 10, so N1 wins.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** N2 occupied only ~10 sec; it's not the majority stage.

**C.** Epochs are not subdivided by AASM rules; the entire epoch receives a single stage score under the majority rule.

**D.** Wake is incorrect because the EEG shows sleep features and alpha does not dominate.

Exam Trap

Don't score N2 just because a spindle appears at the very end. Apply the majority rule: which stage occupies \>15 sec?

Memory Anchor

One epoch = one stage. The stage occupying \>15 sec (\>50%) wins.

Rule Applied

AASM: When an epoch contains two or more stages, score as the stage comprising the greatest portion of the epoch.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
An epoch on a PSG recording shows low chin EMG and conjugate rapid eye movements for the first 20 seconds. In the last 10 seconds, both a sleep spindle and a K-complex appear.

What is the correct sleep stage for this entire epoch?

options.text: Stage REM for the entire epoch
Stage N2 for the entire epoch
Stage REM for 20 sec, N2 for 10 sec
Stage N1 for the entire epoch

rationales.whyCorrect:
Although the first 20 sec show low chin EMG and REMs (consistent with REM), the last 10 sec contain both a sleep spindle and K-complex. Per AASM, presence of a K-complex or spindle in any epoch mandates N2, regardless of the remainder. This rule takes precedence over the majority rule.

**Clue in the question.** A sleep spindle AND K-complex appear — both are definitive N2 markers that override REM-like appearance.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Adult sleep stage scoring (N2 markers override REM)
rationales.eli10:
The trump card rule again. First 2/3 looks like REM, but the moment a spindle or K-complex shows up, the whole window is N2. It's like a referee's whistle — the N2 waveforms stop the play and declare N2.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** REM is excluded because the epoch contains a spindle and K-complex, which never occur in REM.

**C.** AASM rules do not subdivide epochs; a single stage score is assigned.

**D.** N1 is incorrect because spindles/K-complexes are present, moving the floor to at least N2.

Exam Trap

The majority rule does not apply when definitive markers (K-complexes, spindles) are present. Their presence overrides majority.

Memory Anchor

K-complex or spindle anywhere in the epoch = N2. The trump card beats the majority rule.

Rule Applied

AASM: An epoch containing K-complex(es) or spindle(s) is scored N2, even if REMs and low chin EMG are present.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
During an epoch scored as N2, a technologist observes an abrupt shift in EEG frequency to alpha and theta activity that lasts 5 seconds. The preceding 10 seconds consist of stable N2 sleep. There is no concurrent increase in chin EMG amplitude.

How should this event be scored?

options.text: As an arousal
As a change in sleep stage to N1
As a change in sleep stage to Wake
This event should not be scored

rationales.whyCorrect:
AASM defines a NREM arousal as an abrupt EEG frequency shift including alpha, theta, and/or \>16 Hz (not spindles), lasting \>=3 sec, preceded by \>=10 sec stable sleep. This 5-sec shift includes alpha/theta, is abrupt, and has 10 sec stable N2 before it. No concurrent chin EMG increase is required in NREM.

**Clue in the question.** Abrupt EEG shift lasting 5 sec, preceded by 10 sec stable sleep — meets the 3-sec minimum for NREM arousals.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Arousal scoring in NREM sleep
rationales.eli10:
An arousal is a brief wake-up call inside sleep. The brain shifts to faster waves for \>=3 sec, but you don't fully wake. For NREM arousals, only the EEG shift is needed; chin EMG doesn't have to change. In REM, BOTH EEG shift AND chin EMG increase are required.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** A single arousal does not change the sleep stage of the epoch; it's scored as an event within the epoch.

**C.** The epoch remains N2 despite the arousal; arousals don't change the stage.

**D.** Incorrect because the event meets all arousal criteria.

Exam Trap

Do not require a chin EMG increase for NREM arousals. That requirement applies ONLY to REM sleep arousals.

Memory Anchor

NREM arousal = abrupt EEG shift \>=3 sec, no EMG requirement. REM arousal = EEG shift \>=3 sec AND chin EMG increase \>=1 sec.

Rule Applied

AASM NREM arousal: abrupt EEG frequency shift (alpha/theta/\>16 Hz) \>=3 sec, preceded by \>=10 sec stable sleep.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
While reviewing an N2 epoch, a technologist notes an abrupt EEG frequency shift lasting 2.5 seconds that includes alpha activity. The shift follows 10 seconds of stable sleep, and the chin EMG increases transiently during the shift.

Should this be scored as an arousal?

options.text: Yes, because it includes alpha activity
Yes, because the chin EMG increased
No, because the frequency shift is less than 3 seconds
No, because the patient remained in N2

rationales.whyCorrect:
The EEG frequency shift lasts only 2.5 sec, short of the 3-sec minimum for scoring an arousal under AASM rules. Even though the shift includes alpha, chin EMG increases transiently, and the event follows 10 sec stable sleep, the duration criterion is absolute. If \<3 sec, no arousal is scored regardless of other features.

**Clue in the question.** The frequency shift lasts 2.5 seconds — the minimum for any arousal is 3 seconds.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Arousal scoring (minimum duration)
rationales.eli10:
The arousal rule has a strict stopwatch: the brain wave change must last \>=3 full seconds. 2.5 sec is too short to count, even if it looks like one and the chin tightens. Think of holding a note for 3 beats; 2.5 doesn't qualify.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** The EEG shift must exceed 3 sec, not merely 2 sec. 2.5 sec is insufficient.

**B.** Chin EMG increase is not a criterion for NREM arousal scoring; it's required only in REM.

**D.** While the patient remained in N2, this is not the primary reason — the duration is the deciding factor.

Exam Trap

Do not be distracted by chin EMG changes during NREM. Focus on the EEG duration: is it \>=3 sec?

Memory Anchor

Arousal = abrupt EEG shift \>=3 sec + 10 sec stable sleep before it. No exceptions on duration.

Rule Applied

AASM: The abrupt shift in EEG frequency must last \>=3 sec to be scored as an arousal.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
During a REM sleep epoch, a technologist observes an abrupt EEG frequency shift lasting 4 seconds. The chin EMG amplitude increases transiently but the increase lasts only 0.5 seconds.

How should this event be scored?

options.text: As a REM arousal
As a transition to N1
As a transition to Wake
It should not be scored as an arousal

rationales.whyCorrect:
During REM, AASM requires BOTH an abrupt EEG frequency shift \>=3 sec AND a concurrent chin EMG increase \>=1 sec. The EEG shift lasts 4 sec (meets criterion), but chin EMG increases only 0.5 sec (below 1-sec minimum). Because the EMG criterion is not satisfied, this does not qualify as a REM arousal.

**Clue in the question.** In REM, the chin EMG increase must last at least 1 second; 0.5 seconds is too short.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Arousal scoring (REM-specific criteria)
rationales.eli10:
Scoring an arousal in REM is harder than NREM: you need BOTH brain wave speed-up for \>=3 sec AND chin tightening for \>=1 sec. Here the brain shift lasted 4 sec but the chin only tightened for half a second. Not enough — no arousal.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Not scored because chin EMG increase \<1 sec.

**B.** Transition to N1 would require sustained LAMF without REMs and higher EMG — not described.

**C.** Transition to wake would need alpha \>50% or eye blinks with high EMG — none present.

Exam Trap

In REM, do NOT score an arousal based on EEG change alone. Verify the chin EMG increase lasts \>=1 full second.

Memory Anchor

REM arousal = EEG shift \>=3 sec AND chin EMG \>=1 sec. BOTH required. NREM arousal = EEG shift \>=3 sec only.

Rule Applied

AASM REM arousal: abrupt EEG frequency shift \>=3 sec AND concurrent chin EMG amplitude increase \>=1 sec.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A respiratory event is observed during N2 sleep. The nasal pressure and thermal sensor show a 92% drop from baseline lasting 14 seconds. The respiratory effort channels (thoracic and abdominal belts) demonstrate continued effort throughout the event. A 4% oxygen desaturation is associated.

How should this event be classified?

options.text: Central apnea
Obstructive apnea
Mixed apnea
Hypopnea

rationales.whyCorrect:
Airflow drops 92% (\>=90% apnea threshold) for 14 sec (\>=10 sec minimum). Respiratory effort channels show continued effort throughout. When airflow is nearly absent while effort persists, the event is obstructive apnea — the airway is blocked but the patient continues trying to breathe. The 4% desaturation further supports clinical significance.

**Clue in the question.** Airflow drops \>=90% with continued respiratory effort — the defining pattern of obstructive apnea.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Respiratory event scoring (obstructive apnea)
rationales.eli10:
An obstructive apnea is like trying to drink a thick milkshake through a collapsed straw. Your mouth works (chest/belly moving = effort) but nothing gets through because the straw is pinched (airway blocked = no airflow).

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Central apnea shows absent effort on both channels; effort is present here.

**C.** Mixed apnea shows initial absent effort then effort resumes; effort is present throughout here.

**D.** Hypopnea requires only a 30%+ drop, but 92% meets the higher 90% apnea threshold.

Exam Trap

Don't confuse the 30% hypopnea threshold with the 90% apnea threshold. \>=90% drop is apnea, not hypopnea.

Memory Anchor

Apnea = airflow drop \>=90% for \>=10 sec. Effort present = obstructive. Effort absent = central. Effort absent then present = mixed.

Rule Applied

AASM: Score apnea when peak signal drops \>=90% of baseline for \>=10 sec. Classify as obstructive if inspiratory effort continues throughout.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
During a PSG, a technologist notes a 95% reduction in airflow lasting 12 seconds on both the thermal sensor and nasal pressure transducer. The thoracic and abdominal effort belts show paradoxical (out-of-phase) movement throughout the event.

What type of respiratory event is this?

options.text: Central apnea
Obstructive apnea
Mixed apnea
Hypopnea

rationales.whyCorrect:
Airflow drops 95% (\>=90%) for 12 sec (\>=10 sec). Thoracic and abdominal effort show paradoxical (out-of-phase) movement, indicating continued effort against an obstructed airway. Paradoxical thoracoabdominal movement is a classic sign of upper airway obstruction during sleep.

**Clue in the question.** Paradoxical (out-of-phase) chest and abdominal movement during absent airflow — this is obstructive effort.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Respiratory event scoring (obstructive with paradoxical effort)
rationales.eli10:
When the airway is blocked, chest and belly can fight each other — chest expands while belly sucks in. This see-saw motion (paradoxical breathing) proves the person IS trying to breathe (not central) but the airway IS blocked (obstructive).

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Central apnea requires absent effort on both belts; paradoxical movement indicates effort IS present.

**C.** Mixed apnea requires initial absent effort then effort; effort is present throughout.

**D.** Hypopnea requires 30-89% drop; 95% meets the apnea threshold.

Exam Trap

Paradoxical breathing = effort = obstructive apnea (not central). Do not misinterpret paradoxical movement as absent effort.

Memory Anchor

Paradoxical thoracoabdominal movement = airway obstruction with continued effort = obstructive apnea.

Rule Applied

AASM: Score as obstructive apnea when inspiratory effort is present (including paradoxical movement) throughout the entire period of absent airflow.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A technologist identifies a 90% drop in airflow lasting 13 seconds. Both the thoracic and abdominal respiratory effort channels show an absence of signal throughout the entire 13-second period.

How should this event be classified?

options.text: Central apnea
Obstructive apnea
Mixed apnea
Hypopnea

rationales.whyCorrect:
Airflow drops 90% for 13 sec (\>=10 sec). BOTH thoracic and abdominal effort channels show absence of signal throughout the entire event. When no respiratory effort exists during absent airflow, the apnea is central — the CNS drive to breathe is temporarily absent or reduced.

**Clue in the question.** BOTH effort channels show an absence of signal throughout the entire event — no effort at all means central apnea.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, and Data Verification — Respiratory event scoring (central apnea)
rationales.eli10:
A central apnea is like the brain forgetting to tell the body to breathe. Both chest and belly stay still — no effort at all. The technologist sees flat lines on both belts the whole time airflow is zero.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** Obstructive apnea requires continued effort during airflow absence; both belts are flat here.

**C.** Mixed apnea requires absent effort then effort; effort is absent throughout.

**D.** Hypopnea requires only 30%+ drop; 90% exceeds the apnea threshold.

Exam Trap

If both effort belts are flat during an apnea, it's central. If even one belt shows effort, look more carefully.

Memory Anchor

No airflow + no effort on BOTH belts = central apnea. No airflow + effort present = obstructive apnea.

Rule Applied

AASM: Score as central apnea when absent inspiratory effort throughout the entire period of absent airflow.
