subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A technologist is performing impedance checks before starting a PSG. The impedance for the C3 electrode reads 8 kOhms, while all other EEG electrodes read below 5 kOhms.

What is the MOST appropriate action?

options.text: Proceed with the study since 8 kOhms is acceptable for EEG recording.
Remove the electrode, re-prep the site, and reapply the electrode to achieve impedance below 5 kOhms to minimize environmental noise and match other electrodes.
Increase the impedance threshold setting on the amplifier to accept 8 kOhms.
Replace the gold cup electrode with a different type.

rationales.whyCorrect:
AASM recommendations state that EEG electrode impedances should be below 5 kOhms for optimal signal quality. An impedance of 8 kOhms on a single electrode creates an impedance mismatch with the other electrodes, which increases susceptibility to environmental electrical noise (particularly 60 Hz interference) and degrades common-mode rejection. Re-preparing the site and reapplying the electrode is a standard troubleshooting step that is quick, safe, and effective.

**Clue in the question.** 8 kOhms exceeds the recommended threshold of less than 5 kOhms, and all other electrodes are below 5 kOhms.

Domain 2: Study Preparation and Performance — EEG electrode impedance management
rationales.eli10:
EEG electrodes work best when they all have similarly low electrical resistance to the skin — think of it like all having equally clean windows to look through. If one window is dirty (high impedance), that channel is more likely to pick up static and interference. The technologist should clean that spot and reapply the electrode to get it below 5 kOhms.

ELI Example

Like having one foggy window in a car — you clean it so you can see as clearly as through the others.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** While 8 kOhms may still record a signal, it is above the recommended 5 kOhms threshold and creates an impedance mismatch that degrades recording quality.

**C.** Changing the amplifier threshold masks the problem instead of fixing it; proper electrode application is the correct approach.

**D.** Replacing the electrode type is unnecessary — the issue is site preparation and application, not the electrode hardware.

Exam Trap

Assuming that any impedance under 10 kOhms is acceptable because some older guidelines used a 10 kOhm threshold. Current AASM standards recommend less than 5 kOhms.

Memory Anchor

EEG impedance goal = below 5 kOhms for all electrodes. Re-prep if above.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A patient calls the sleep laboratory two days after their PSG and states, "My face is broken out in a rash where the electrodes were placed. What should I do?"

What is the technologist's BEST response?

options.text: Advise the patient that mild skin irritation can occur from electrode paste and recommend gentle cleansing; document the call and notify the supervising clinician if symptoms persist or worsen.
Tell the patient this is a normal reaction and no follow-up is needed.
Instruct the patient to apply hydrocortisone cream immediately.
Advise the patient to go to the emergency department.

rationales.whyCorrect:
This is the appropriate balance of patient education, reassurance, documentation, and clinical escalation. Mild skin irritation from electrode paste or collodion is a known, generally benign occurrence. The technologist provides practical self-care advice (gentle cleansing), fulfills the documentation obligation, and establishes the appropriate escalation pathway (notify clinician if symptoms persist). This response operates within the technologist's scope of practice.

**Clue in the question.** The patient describes a "rash" two days after electrode placement — a timeframe consistent with contact irritation from electrode products.

Domain 1: Clinical Overview, Education, Patient Support — Post-study patient follow-up and education
rationales.eli10:
Sometimes the gel and paste used to stick electrodes to the skin can cause a mild rash, like when a bandage irritates your skin. The technologist can tell the patient to wash their face gently and that the rash should go away on its own. But they also write down what happened and let the doctor know, in case it gets worse and needs more treatment.

ELI Example

Like a mild reaction to a new soap — wash it off, watch it, and call the doctor if it does not improve.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** Dismissing the patient's concern without documentation or follow-up instructions is inappropriate and fails to address potential clinical issues.

**C.** Recommending a medication (hydrocortisone) is outside the technologist's scope of practice; medication recommendations must come from a licensed clinician.

**D.** A mild rash does not warrant an emergency department visit; this over-escalates a typically minor issue.

Exam Trap

Over-escalating (sending to ED) or under-escalating (dismissing without documentation). The correct answer balances patient education, documentation, and appropriate clinical follow-up.

Memory Anchor

Post-study rash = educate, document, notify clinician if persistent. Stay in scope of practice.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A patient on CPAP at 12 cm H₂O develops central apneas during NREM sleep. These central apneas were not present on the diagnostic portion of the study. Obstructive events are well controlled.

What is the MOST appropriate intervention?

options.text: Reduce the CPAP pressure gradually to see if the central apneas resolve at a lower pressure, as these may be therapy-emergent central apneas that are pressure-dependent.
Continue at 12 cm H₂O and add supplemental oxygen.
Immediately switch to bilevel PAP with a backup rate.
Discontinue PAP therapy entirely and end the study.

rationales.whyCorrect:
The development of central apneas during CPAP titration that were not present on the diagnostic study strongly suggests therapy-emergent central sleep apnea (TECSA), also known as complex sleep apnea. TECSA is often pressure-dependent — higher CPAP pressures can trigger central apneas through increased ventilatory drive and CO₂ washout. The first-line approach is gradual pressure reduction, as many patients have a pressure window where obstructive events are controlled without inducing central apneas. If pressure reduction fails, then advanced modalities (bilevel ST, ASV) are considered.

**Clue in the question.** Central apneas appear at therapeutic pressure and were absent on the diagnostic study — the hallmark of therapy-emergent central apneas.

Domain 4: Treatment and Intervention — Management of therapy-emergent central sleep apnea (TECSA)
rationales.eli10:
Sometimes CPAP pressure that is high enough to keep the throat open can also trick the brain into thinking it does not need to breathe, causing "central" pauses where the brain simply does not send the "breathe" signal. The first thing to try is lowering the pressure a little — there might be a sweet spot where the throat stays open but the brain keeps breathing on its own.

ELI Example

Like finding the right water temperature in a shower — too hot (high pressure) causes a problem, so you turn it down a bit to find the comfortable spot.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** Supplemental oxygen may help hypoxemia but does not address the underlying pressure-dependent mechanism of TECSA. Pressure reduction should be attempted first.

**C.** Jumping immediately to bilevel ST with backup rate is premature — pressure reduction is the first-line approach for TECSA.

**D.** Discontinuing therapy entirely is not appropriate when obstructive events are controlled and a treatable explanation (pressure-dependent central apneas) exists.

Exam Trap

Assuming that central apneas during CPAP always require advanced PAP modalities. TECSA often resolves with simple pressure reduction, which is the recommended first step.

Memory Anchor

TECSA = new centrals on CPAP → try lower pressure first, then consider bilevel ST/ASV.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
An adult PSG epoch shows REMs, low chin EMG tone, and a sawtooth wave pattern on the EEG. The epoch also contains an apnea event that meets criteria for scoring.

How should this epoch be staged?

options.text: Stage REM — the presence of REMs, low chin tone, and sawtooth waves is consistent with REM sleep; the apnea does not change the stage.
Stage N2, because the apnea indicates the patient is not in REM sleep.
Stage N1, because apneas are only scored in N1 sleep.
Stage Wake, because apneas only occur during wakefulness.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Sleep staging is based on EEG, EOG, and chin EMG patterns — not on respiratory events. The epoch exhibits the defining features of REM sleep: rapid eye movements, low chin EMG tone, and sawtooth waves on EEG. The presence of an apnea does not alter the sleep stage. Respiratory events are scored independently from sleep staging; they can occur in any stage of sleep including REM. The AASM manual is clear that respiratory events are scored separately and do not affect the determination of sleep stage.

**Clue in the question.** The epoch has all three hallmarks of REM sleep (REMs, low chin tone, sawtooth waves). Apneas are scored independently of sleep stage.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, Data Verification — Sleep stage scoring in the presence of respiratory events
rationales.eli10:
Sleep stage is determined by what the brain, eyes, and chin muscles are doing — not by breathing. If all the signs point to REM sleep (eye movements, relaxed muscles, specific brain wave patterns), it stays REM even if the patient has a breathing pause during that time. Breathing events and sleep stage are scored separately.

ELI Example

If you are watching a movie (REM sleep) and someone pauses it (apnea), you are still watching a movie — the pause does not change what you are doing.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** The presence of an apnea does not change REM to N2. N2 requires sleep spindles or K-complexes, which are not described.

**C.** Apneas can be scored in any sleep stage, not only N1. Additionally, the epoch does not meet N1 criteria (it has REM features).

**D.** Apneas commonly occur during sleep, not wakefulness, and this epoch has clear sleep features (low chin EMG, sawtooth waves).

Exam Trap

Letting a respiratory event override sleep staging criteria. Sleep stage and respiratory events are scored independently — the presence of one does not determine the other.

Memory Anchor

Sleep stage is from EEG/EOG/EMG. Respiratory events are scored separately. They do not change each other.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
During a PSG recording, the technologist notices a rhythmic 60 Hz artifact appearing across all EEG channels simultaneously.

What is the MOST likely cause of this artifact?

options.text: Electrical interference from an inadequately grounded device in the patient's room, or high electrode impedance allowing environmental line noise to contaminate the recording.
The patient is experiencing a generalized seizure.
The patient is in Stage N3 sleep with high-amplitude delta activity.
The reference electrode has become completely disconnected.

rationales.whyCorrect:
A rhythmic 60 Hz artifact appearing simultaneously across all EEG channels is the classic signature of electrical line noise (60 Hz in North America, 50 Hz in Europe). This occurs when environmental electrical interference is picked up by the recording system, typically due to high electrode impedances, inadequate grounding, or nearby electrical equipment. The simultaneous appearance across all channels distinguishes it from physiological signals (which would have localized or asymmetric patterns).

**Clue in the question.** "60 Hz artifact" and "across all EEG channels simultaneously" — this is the definition of electrical line noise contamination.

Domain 2: Study Preparation and Performance — Troubleshooting artifacts during PSG recording
rationales.eli10:
The electricity in the walls of buildings runs at 60 cycles per second (60 Hz). If the EEG equipment is not properly grounded or if the electrodes have high resistance, this electrical hum can leak into the recording and show up as a fast, rhythmic wavy line on all channels at the same time. It is like radio static — it is coming from the environment, not from the patient's brain.

ELI Example

Like hearing a buzz on a radio when standing too close to a power line — the buzz is from the environment, not from the radio station.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** A generalized seizure produces high-amplitude, evolving patterns that change over time — not a constant 60 Hz rhythm across all channels.

**C.** Stage N3 slow wave activity is 0.5-2 Hz with high amplitude — very different from 60 Hz, which is much faster.

**D.** A disconnected reference would produce a saturated or wandering baseline, not a clean 60 Hz rhythmic artifact.

Exam Trap

Misinterpreting 60 Hz artifact as seizure activity or deep sleep. The key discriminating feature is the frequency (60 Hz) and simultaneous appearance across all channels.

Memory Anchor

60 Hz on all channels = line noise. Check grounding, impedances, and nearby electrical equipment.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
During a pre-study phone call, a patient asks the technologist, "Will this sleep study tell me if I have sleep apnea?"

What is the MOST appropriate response within the technologist's scope of practice?

options.text: "Yes, I will be able to tell you your diagnosis when you wake up in the morning."
"The study measures your breathing, brain waves, and other signals; I can tell you what I see on the recording before you leave."
"Sleep studies cannot diagnose sleep apnea — only a blood test can."
"The study records comprehensive physiological data during sleep; the interpreting physician will review the results and provide a diagnosis to your referring provider."

rationales.whyCorrect:
Sleep technologists are not licensed to diagnose medical conditions. The technologist's role is to perform high-quality recordings and provide technical observations — not to interpret results or render diagnoses. This response accurately describes what the study does, clarifies the technologist's role, and correctly identifies that the interpreting physician provides the diagnosis. It is honest, within scope of practice, and sets appropriate patient expectations.

**Clue in the question.** The question explicitly asks about response "within the technologist's scope of practice."

Domain 1: Clinical Overview, Education, Patient Support — Patient education within scope of practice
rationales.eli10:
The sleep technologist runs the test but is not the doctor who reads the results. It is like a medical lab — the technician draws the blood, but the doctor tells you what the results mean. The technologist can explain what the study measures but cannot give a diagnosis. The doctor reviews everything and tells your regular doctor what was found.

ELI Example

The X-ray technician takes the picture but does not tell you if your bone is broken — the radiologist does that.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** This oversteps the technologist's scope of practice by implying the technologist can provide a diagnosis.

**B.** While more restrained than A, this implies the technologist will provide clinical interpretation ("what I see") before the physician reviews the study.

**C.** This is factually incorrect — PSG is the gold standard for diagnosing sleep apnea; blood tests cannot diagnose it.

Exam Trap

Selecting an answer that sounds helpful but exceeds the technologist's scope of practice. Technologists must not diagnose — they describe, record, and report.

Memory Anchor

Technologist scope = describe the test, not the diagnosis. "The physician will interpret."

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A patient with complex sleep apnea (predominantly obstructive apneas on diagnostic study, developing central apneas during CPAP titration) does not respond to pressure reduction. The central apneas persist at lower pressures.

What is the MOST appropriate next treatment consideration?

options.text: Continue CPAP at the highest tolerated pressure.
Discharge the patient without therapy.
Add supplemental oxygen at 5 L/min to the CPAP circuit.
Transition to bilevel PAP with a backup rate (bilevel ST) or adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV) under the supervising clinician's guidance.

rationales.whyCorrect:
When therapy-emergent central apneas persist despite pressure reduction, the patient meets criteria for complex sleep apnea. Standard CPAP cannot address the central component. Bilevel PAP with a backup rate (bilevel ST) ensures a minimum respiratory rate by delivering timed breaths when the patient fails to initiate them. Adaptive servo-ventilation (ASV) provides dynamic pressure support that stabilizes ventilation and addresses the periodic breathing pattern. Either modality is appropriate, with the choice depending on patient characteristics and clinician preference.

**Clue in the question.** Central apneas persist at lower pressures after being absent on diagnostic study — this defines complex sleep apnea requiring advanced PAP modalities.

Domain 4: Treatment and Intervention — Management of complex sleep apnea refractory to pressure reduction
rationales.eli10:
When lowering the pressure does not fix the central breathing pauses, a more advanced machine is needed. These machines can sense when the patient stops trying to breathe and give an extra push of air to remind the lungs to work. One type (bilevel ST) delivers breaths on a timer; another (ASV) adjusts the amount of air support breath by breath.

ELI Example

Like upgrading from cruise control (basic CPAP) to autopilot (ASV) when the road gets too complicated for simple speed maintenance.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Continuing CPAP when the patient has documented complex sleep apnea with persistent central events is ineffective and does not address the underlying pathophysiology.

**B.** Discharging without therapy is inappropriate when effective PAP modalities (bilevel ST, ASV) are available to treat this condition.

**C.** Supplemental oxygen alone does not address the central apnea mechanism and is not first-line therapy for complex sleep apnea.

Exam Trap

Thinking that supplemental oxygen is the next step after failed pressure reduction for complex sleep apnea. The correct progression is: reduce pressure → if centrals persist, transition to advanced PAP modality (bilevel ST or ASV).

Memory Anchor

Complex sleep apnea refractory to pressure reduction = bilevel ST or ASV.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
During scoring of an adult PSG, the technologist encounters an epoch with the following characteristics: posterior dominant rhythm (alpha) present for more than 50% of the epoch, rapid eye movements, eye blinks, and high chin EMG tone. A K-complex is also present in this epoch.

How should this epoch be staged?

options.text: Stage N2, because a K-complex is present.
Stage N1, because K-complexes can occur in N1.
Stage REM, because K-complexes can appear during phasic REM.

Stage W (Wake) — when alpha rhythm occupies more than 50% of the epoch with high chin tone, the epoch is scored as Wake; an isolated K-complex in an otherwise Wake epoch does not override the Wake designation.

rationales.whyCorrect:
AASM rules for scoring Wake require that when the posterior dominant rhythm (alpha) occupies more than 50% of the epoch, the epoch is scored as Stage W, regardless of other features that might suggest sleep. The presence of rapid eye movements, eye blinks, and high chin EMG tone all support the Wake designation. An isolated K-complex can occasionally appear during drowsy wakefulness and does not by itself define N2 sleep — N2 requires K-complexes in the context of a sleep epoch without Wake-defining features.

**Clue in the question.** Alpha rhythm occupies more than 50% of the epoch — the primary AASM criterion for scoring Wake.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, Data Verification — Sleep-wake staging with ambiguous features
rationales.eli10:
The brain produces a specific rhythm (alpha waves) when you are awake with your eyes closed. If more than half the 30-second window shows this wakefulness rhythm, the technologist scores it as "awake" — even if there is one sleep wave (K-complex) mixed in. It is like one raindrop does not mean it is raining — you need the full pattern.

ELI Example

One snowflake does not make it winter. One K-complex in a mostly-awake brain does not make it sleep.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** An isolated K-complex in an epoch where alpha rhythm occupies more than 50% does not establish N2 sleep. N2 requires that the epoch first be scored as sleep (alpha less than 50%).

**B.** N1 requires low-amplitude mixed-frequency activity with alpha occupying less than 50% of the epoch — opposite of what is described.

**C.** REM sleep has low chin EMG tone (not high) and does not feature K-complexes — K-complexes are an NREM phenomenon.

Exam Trap

Seeing a K-complex and automatically scoring N2 without first checking whether the epoch meets Wake criteria. The AASM staging hierarchy prioritizes Wake criteria over N2 criteria.

Memory Anchor

Alpha \>50% of epoch + high chin tone = Wake. K-complexes in Wake do not make it N2.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A technologist is placing EOG electrodes for a standard PSG montage.

Which of the following placements conforms to AASM recommendations?

options.text: E1 and E2 are both placed 1 cm above the outer canthi.
E1 is placed 1 cm below the left outer canthus and E2 is placed 1 cm above the right outer canthus, both referenced to the forehead.
Both electrodes are placed on the nasion.
E1 is placed 1 cm below the left outer canthus and E2 is placed 1 cm above the right outer canthus, with both referenced to the same mastoid or linked mastoid reference.

rationales.whyCorrect:
AASM recommended EOG placement positions E1 (left eye electrode) 1 cm below the left outer canthus and E2 (right eye electrode) 1 cm above the right outer canthus. This offset placement (one above, one below) produces out-of-phase deflections during vertical eye movements because the cornea is positively charged relative to the retina. When the eyes move, each electrode detects the movement in opposite polarity, creating the characteristic out-of-phase pattern used to identify eye movements. Both are referenced to the same mastoid or linked mastoids.

**Clue in the question.** "Conforms to AASM recommendations" — the AASM specifies the 1 cm above/below offset placement.

Domain 2: Study Preparation and Performance — EOG electrode placement per AASM recommendations
rationales.eli10:
The technologist places one electrode just below the left eye and one just above the right eye. Because the front of the eyeball has a different electrical charge than the back, when the eyes move up and down, the two electrodes see opposite signals. This creates a distinctive "see-saw" pattern on the recording that makes it easy to spot eye movements during sleep.

ELI Example

Like two people watching a parade from opposite sides of the street — one sees the float go left-to-right, the other sees it go right-to-left. Their descriptions are "out of phase" but describe the same event.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Placing both electrodes above the canthi would produce in-phase deflections, making it difficult to distinguish eye movements from EEG artifact.

**B.** Referencing to the forehead is not the AASM standard — mastoid references (M1, M2) are used.

**C.** Placing electrodes on the nasion would not capture eye movements effectively and is not an AASM-recognized placement.

Exam Trap

Confusing the correct EOG placement (offset: one below, one above) with incorrect symmetric placements (both above or both below). The offset is essential for out-of-phase recordings.

Memory Anchor

E1 = 1 cm below left outer canthus, E2 = 1 cm above right outer canthus. Mastoid reference. Offset creates out-of-phase deflections.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A 67-year-old patient with moderate dementia is brought to the sleep laboratory by their adult child for an attended PSG. The patient is agitated and repeatedly asks to go home.

What is the MOST appropriate approach?

options.text: Proceed with the full hookup while gently restraining the patient for safety.
Attempt gentle redirection and reassurance; involve the caregiver in the setup process; if the patient cannot be calmed, notify the supervising clinician to discuss whether the study should proceed.
Administer a sedative from the laboratory's standing medication supply.
Discharge the patient immediately without attempting the study.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Patients with dementia may become agitated in unfamiliar environments. The appropriate approach uses de-escalation techniques (gentle redirection, reassurance), leverages the caregiver's presence as a calming influence, and includes a clear escalation pathway (notify clinician) if behavioral management is unsuccessful. This approach respects patient dignity, prioritizes safety, and maintains clinical communication. The technologist should not physically restrain, sedate without orders, or discharge without attempting the study.

**Clue in the question.** Patient has moderate dementia, is agitated, and a caregiver is present — each element guides the management approach.

Domain 1: Clinical Overview, Education, Patient Support — Managing agitated or cognitively impaired patients
rationales.eli10:
When a patient with memory problems becomes scared and upset in an unfamiliar place, the technologist should stay calm and reassuring. Having a family member nearby is very helpful because familiar faces reduce anxiety. If the patient simply cannot settle down, the technologist calls the doctor to decide if the study should continue or be rescheduled.

ELI Example

Like helping a scared child at the dentist — you stay calm, let the parent hold their hand, and if it becomes too much, you stop and make a new plan.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Physical restraint is never appropriate for managing agitation in the sleep laboratory — it is traumatic, unethical, and can escalate the situation.

**C.** Administering medication without a specific order is outside the technologist's scope of practice and potentially dangerous.

**D.** Immediate discharge without attempting any de-escalation or clinical consultation prematurely abandons the patient's care.

Exam Trap

Selecting immediate discharge (D) as the "safest" option without recognizing that attempting de-escalation with caregiver involvement is the appropriate first step.

Memory Anchor

Dementia + agitation = redirect, involve caregiver, notify clinician if unsuccessful. No restraint, no un-prescribed sedation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A patient on CPAP at 11 cm H₂O has well-controlled obstructive events, but the SpO₂ remains at 87% despite adequate PAP therapy. The technologist has a standing order to add supplemental oxygen.

At what flow rate should oxygen typically be initiated in this scenario?

options.text: 5 L/min, as higher flow rates are needed during PAP therapy.
0.5 L/min, as even small amounts of oxygen can cause oxygen toxicity.
1 L/min, with titration upward in 1 L/min increments based on SpO₂ response, following the laboratory protocol and standing order.
10 L/min to rapidly correct the desaturation.

rationales.whyCorrect:
When adding supplemental oxygen during PAP therapy, standard practice is to begin at a low flow rate (typically 1 L/min) and titrate upward in 1 L/min increments while monitoring SpO₂ response. This conservative approach minimizes the risk of oxygen toxicity or excessive FiO₂ while achieving the therapeutic goal (typically SpO₂ greater than or equal to 90%). The technologist must follow the laboratory's written protocol and the standing order from the supervising clinician.

**Clue in the question.** The technologist "has a standing order" and the question asks at what rate to "initiate" oxygen — both point to starting low and titrating.

Domain 4: Treatment and Intervention — Supplemental oxygen administration during PAP therapy
rationales.eli10:
When extra oxygen is needed during CPAP, you start with a small amount — just 1 liter per minute — and check if the oxygen level in the blood improves enough. If not, you add another liter, then check again. This step-by-step approach keeps the patient safe and finds the lowest amount of oxygen that does the job.

ELI Example

Like adding salt to soup — you add a little, taste, add more if needed. You never dump the whole container in at once.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Starting at 5 L/min is too aggressive; the standard starting flow rate is 1 L/min with upward titration.

**B.** 0.5 L/min is too low to achieve clinically meaningful increases in FiO₂ for most patients. Oxygen toxicity is not a concern at low flow rates used during PAP titration.

**D.** 10 L/min is an excessively high starting rate that could cause hyperoxia and is not indicated for routine SpO₂ correction during PAP titration.

Exam Trap

Assuming that because PAP therapy dilutes the oxygen, a high starting flow rate is needed. The correct approach is to start at 1 L/min and titrate based on response.

Memory Anchor

O₂ during PAP = start at 1 L/min, titrate up 1 L/min at a time per protocol and SpO₂.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A technologist is scoring a respiratory event in an adult PSG. The nasal pressure signal shows a drop of greater than or equal to 90% of the pre-event baseline lasting 12 seconds. The respiratory effort channels show continued effort throughout the event.

How should this event be classified?

options.text: Central apnea
Mixed apnea
Obstructive apnea
Hypopnea

rationales.whyCorrect:
An obstructive apnea is defined by a drop in the airflow signal of greater than or equal to 90% of baseline lasting at least 10 seconds, with continued or increased respiratory effort throughout the event. This event meets all criteria: greater than or equal to 90% amplitude reduction, 12-second duration (meets the 10-second minimum), and continued respiratory effort. The continued effort distinguishes obstructive apnea from central apnea (absent effort) and mixed apnea (initial central followed by obstructive component).

**Clue in the question.** "Respiratory effort channels show continued effort throughout the event" — this is the defining feature of obstructive apnea.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, Data Verification — Classification of respiratory events
rationales.eli10:
When the airway collapses during sleep, the brain keeps trying to breathe — the chest and belly keep moving. But no air gets through because the throat is blocked. This is an obstructive apnea. The key difference from a central apnea is that in central apnea, the brain does not even try — both airflow and breathing effort stop. Here, the effort continues, telling us it is obstructive.

ELI Example

Like trying to drink a thick milkshake through a collapsed straw — you keep sucking (effort), but nothing comes through (no airflow).

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Central apnea requires absent respiratory effort throughout the event — the opposite of this scenario where effort continues.

**B.** Mixed apnea has a central component (no effort) at the beginning followed by an obstructive component (effort resumes) — not described here.

**D.** Hypopnea requires a drop of at least 30% (not 90% or more), and the drop here meets apnea amplitude criteria.

Exam Trap

Confusing obstructive and central apnea based on airflow patterns alone, without checking the respiratory effort channels. The presence or absence of effort is the key discriminator.

Memory Anchor

Obstructive apnea = no airflow (drop ≥90%) + continued effort. Central apnea = no airflow + no effort.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
During a PSG recording, the technologist observes that the airflow signal from the nasal pressure transducer has suddenly dropped to a flat line, while the thermistor signal continues to show normal airflow.

What is the FIRST troubleshooting step?

options.text: Increase the gain on the nasal pressure channel.
Check whether the nasal cannula has become disconnected from the pressure transducer or has slipped out of the patient's nares.
Replace the thermistor, as it is clearly malfunctioning.
Assume the patient has stopped breathing and initiate emergency protocol.

rationales.whyCorrect:
When one airflow sensor (nasal pressure) shows a flat line while the other (thermistor) continues to show normal airflow, the most likely explanation is a sensor-specific problem rather than a true respiratory event. Nasal pressure cannulas can become disconnected from the transducer, kinked, or displaced from the nares. The thermistor's normal signal confirms the patient is breathing, ruling out a true apnea. The first step is always to check the sensor integrity before escalating.

**Clue in the question.** The discrepancy between the two airflow sensors (flat nasal pressure, normal thermistor) indicates a sensor problem, not a patient problem.

Domain 2: Study Preparation and Performance — Troubleshooting airflow signal loss
rationales.eli10:
When one breathing sensor says "no airflow" but the other says "breathing fine," you should trust the one that is working and fix the one that is not. The nasal cannula probably fell out of the patient's nose or came unplugged. Since the other sensor shows normal breathing, you know the patient is not truly in danger.

ELI Example

If your car's speedometer says 0 mph but you can see you are moving, the problem is with the speedometer, not the car.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Increasing the gain on a flat signal will only amplify the flat line — it does not fix a disconnected sensor.

**C.** The thermistor is functioning correctly (showing normal airflow); there is no indication it is malfunctioning.

**D.** The thermistor confirms the patient is breathing; initiating emergency protocol for a sensor disconnection is an inappropriate overreaction.

Exam Trap

Panicking at a flat airflow signal and assuming the patient has stopped breathing. Always cross-check with the second airflow channel and other physiological signals.

Memory Anchor

One flat airflow channel + other airflow channel normal = sensor problem. Check connection, reposition cannula.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A patient reports during the pre-study interview that they are currently enrolled in a clinical trial for a new insomnia medication. The technologist is not familiar with the trial protocol.

What should the technologist do?

options.text: Proceed with the study as ordered since the clinical trial is unrelated to the PSG.
Ask the patient to discontinue the trial medication for the night of the study.
Document the clinical trial participation and confirm with the ordering clinician that the sleep study protocol is compatible with the trial requirements before proceeding.
Contact the pharmaceutical company sponsoring the trial directly.

rationales.whyCorrect:
A patient's participation in a clinical trial for an insomnia medication is highly relevant to a sleep study. The medication could directly affect sleep architecture, study outcomes, and interpretation. The technologist cannot independently determine whether to proceed — they must document the finding and escalate to the ordering clinician, who can assess compatibility with the trial protocol. The technologist should not ask the patient to discontinue trial medication without clinician authorization, as this could compromise the trial.

**Clue in the question.** The patient is "enrolled in a clinical trial for a new insomnia medication" — a factor that directly impacts sleep study results.

Domain 1: Clinical Overview, Education, Patient Support — Clinical research considerations and communication
rationales.eli10:
If a patient is taking an experimental sleep medication, that drug will change how they sleep during the test — which could mess up both the study results and the clinical trial data. The technologist should write this down and check with the doctor who ordered the sleep study before starting. The doctor needs to make sure the sleep test and the clinical trial do not interfere with each other.

ELI Example

Like a student enrolled in two classes that have conflicting exam schedules — someone needs to coordinate to make sure both can work.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Proceeding without checking compatibility could invalidate the PSG results, compromise the clinical trial, or expose the patient to conflicting protocols.

**B.** The technologist cannot instruct a patient to discontinue a clinical trial medication — this is a clinician-level decision with trial implications.

**D.** Contacting the pharmaceutical company directly is outside the technologist's role and violates privacy and professional boundaries.

Exam Trap

Assuming that an external clinical trial is unrelated to the PSG and proceeding without communication. Any medication or treatment affecting sleep is clinically relevant.

Memory Anchor

Clinical trial participation + sleep study = document, notify ordering clinician, confirm compatibility before proceeding.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A patient who has been successfully titrated on CPAP at 9 cm H₂O begins to exhibit loud snoring and flow limitation when transitioning from NREM to REM sleep. The pressure remains at 9 cm H₂O.

What is the MOST likely explanation and appropriate response?

options.text: The CPAP device is malfunctioning and should be replaced.
The patient likely requires a higher pressure during REM sleep; the technologist should increase pressure in 1 cm H₂O increments during REM to control the events.
Snoring during REM is normal and does not require intervention.
The patient should be switched to an oral appliance immediately.

rationales.whyCorrect:
REM sleep is characterized by generalized muscle atonia, including the upper airway dilator muscles. This makes the airway more collapsible during REM than during NREM, meaning patients often require higher CPAP pressures to maintain airway patency during REM sleep. The development of snoring and flow limitation at a previously effective pressure when transitioning into REM is a classic finding. The appropriate response is to increase pressure during REM to control REM-related events.

**Clue in the question.** Events appear specifically with the transition from NREM to REM at a pressure that was effective during NREM — the hallmark of REM-related OSA.

Domain 4: Treatment and Intervention — REM-related CPAP pressure requirements
rationales.eli10:
During dream sleep (REM), all the muscles in the body become very relaxed, including the throat muscles. This means the airway can collapse more easily than during other sleep stages. A CPAP pressure that works fine during regular sleep may not be strong enough during dream sleep. The technologist needs to increase the pressure while the patient is in REM to keep the airway open.

ELI Example

Like needing a stronger umbrella when the wind picks up — the same umbrella works in light rain (NREM), but you need to hold it tighter in a storm (REM).

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** The device is not malfunctioning — the pressure simply needs to be higher during REM. Replacing the device would not solve the physiological problem.

**C.** Snoring during REM is not normal — it indicates residual upper airway obstruction requiring intervention.

**D.** Switching to an oral appliance during an attended titration study is not appropriate; CPAP titration should continue with pressure adjustment.

Exam Trap

Assuming that a pressure effective in NREM should also be effective in REM. REM sleep physiology makes the airway more collapsible, often requiring higher pressures.

Memory Anchor

REM = muscle atonia = more collapsible airway = often needs higher CPAP pressure. Titrate in REM.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A technologist is scoring an event in an adult PSG. The nasal pressure signal shows a drop of approximately 50% from baseline lasting 15 seconds, associated with a 4% oxygen desaturation from pre-event baseline.

According to the AASM recommended rule (1A), how should this event be classified?

options.text: Hypopnea
Obstructive apnea
Central apnea
Respiratory effort-related arousal (RERA)

rationales.whyCorrect:
Under the AASM recommended hypopnea rule (1A), a hypopnea is scored when the nasal pressure signal drops by greater than or equal to 30% from baseline for at least 10 seconds, associated with a greater than or equal to 3% oxygen desaturation or an arousal. This event meets all criteria: approximately 50% drop (exceeds 30% threshold), 15-second duration (exceeds 10-second minimum), and 4% desaturation (exceeds 3% threshold). A RERA does not meet hypopnea criteria for desaturation or arousal and requires a different definition.

**Clue in the question.** 50% drop from baseline (meets the ≥30% threshold) with 4% desaturation — this matches the AASM 1A hypopnea definition.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, Data Verification — Hypopnea scoring per AASM recommended criteria (Rule 1A)
rationales.eli10:
A hypopnea is a partial blockage of breathing — not a complete stop, but a significant reduction in airflow. The rules say: if airflow drops by at least 30% for at least 10 seconds AND the blood oxygen drops by at least 3%, it counts as a hypopnea. This event drops by about 50% for 15 seconds with a 4% oxygen drop — it checks all the boxes.

ELI Example

Like a garden hose that gets partially kinked — water still flows, but much less than before. If it drops enough and lasts long enough, it counts as a problem.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** An obstructive apnea requires a drop of greater than or equal to 90% — this event drops by only 50%, which does not meet the apnea amplitude threshold.

**C.** A central apnea also requires a drop of greater than or equal to 90% and absent respiratory effort — neither is present here. Additionally, the question does not mention effort channel data.

**D.** A RERA is defined by a sequence of breaths with increasing respiratory effort or flattening of the nasal pressure waveform leading to an arousal, without meeting hypopnea criteria. This event meets hypopnea criteria due to the 4% desaturation.

Exam Trap

Confusing the amplitude thresholds: apnea requires ≥90% drop; hypopnea requires ≥30% drop. A 50% drop is a hypopnea, not an apnea.

Memory Anchor

Hypopnea = airflow drop ≥30%, ≥10 seconds, with ≥3% desaturation or arousal (AASM 1A).

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A technologist is performing calibration procedures before beginning a PSG. During the physiological calibration, the patient is instructed to look left, look right, look up, look down, and blink five times.

What is the PRIMARY purpose of these eye movement calibrations?

options.text: To assess the patient's visual acuity before the study.
To determine whether the patient has nystagmus.
To verify proper EOG electrode placement and polarity by producing characteristic out-of-phase deflections on the recording.
To ensure the patient can follow instructions during the study.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Eye movement calibration during the pre-study physiological calibration serves to confirm that EOG electrodes are correctly placed and wired with the proper polarity. When the patient looks left, the E1 and E2 electrodes produce out-of-phase deflections (one channel deflects upward while the other deflects downward). When they look right, the direction reverses. Looking up and down produces in-phase deflections. These characteristic patterns confirm functional electrode placement and allow the technologist to correct any wiring or placement errors before the study begins.

**Clue in the question.** The question asks for the PRIMARY purpose of eye movement calibrations during PSG setup.

Domain 2: Study Preparation and Performance — Physiological calibration procedures
rationales.eli10:
Before the sleep study starts, the technologist asks the patient to move their eyes in different directions. This is not a vision test — it is to make sure the eye movement sensors are working properly. When you look left, the left sensor should show an up deflection and the right sensor a down deflection. This "see-saw" pattern confirms the sensors are in the right place and wired correctly.

ELI Example

Like doing a sound check before a concert — you are not evaluating the musician's voice, you are making sure the microphone is plugged in and working.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** EOG calibration does not assess visual acuity — it tests electrode function, not the patient's vision.

**B.** While nystagmus might be incidentally noted, detecting nystagmus is not the primary purpose of the calibration procedure.

**D.** While following instructions is reassuring, the primary purpose is technical (verifying electrode function), not behavioral assessment.

Exam Trap

Confusing the purpose of calibration (technical verification of signal quality) with clinical assessment (evaluating the patient's vision or neurological status).

Memory Anchor

Physiological calibration = verify signal quality. EOG cal = check electrode placement and polarity via out-of-phase deflections.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A patient scheduled for a split-night PSG asks the technologist, "What does split-night mean?"

Which explanation is MOST accurate?

options.text: "The first portion of the night is used to diagnose the severity of sleep apnea; if criteria are met, the remainder of the night is used to find a therapeutic PAP pressure."
"Half of the electrodes are placed before midnight and the other half after midnight."
"You will sleep for 4 hours, wake up for 2 hours, then sleep for another 4 hours."
"Two different technologists will monitor you, each for half the night."

rationales.whyCorrect:
A split-night PSG combines diagnostic and therapeutic components in a single night. The study begins as a diagnostic PSG. If the patient demonstrates sufficient obstructive events meeting split-night criteria (typically an AHI greater than or equal to a specified threshold within the first 2 hours of sleep), the technologist initiates CPAP titration for the remainder of the night. This explanation is accurate, clear, and provides the essential information the patient needs in accessible language.

**Clue in the question.** The patient asks for an explanation of what "split-night" means — the answer should define the diagnostic-then-therapeutic sequence.

Domain 1: Clinical Overview, Education, Patient Support — Patient education about split-night protocol
rationales.eli10:
A split-night study does two jobs in one night. During the first part, the technologist watches to see if you have sleep apnea and how bad it is. If the breathing pauses are frequent enough in the first couple of hours, the rest of the night is used to find the right air pressure setting on a CPAP machine to stop the pauses.

ELI Example

Like a two-part job interview — first they see if you qualify (diagnostic), then if you do, they figure out the exact role (titration), all in one visit.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** Split-night refers to the purpose of the study portions, not to electrode application. Electrodes are placed at the beginning and remain throughout the study.

**C.** Split-night does not involve intentionally waking the patient for 2 hours. The split is between diagnostic and therapeutic portions, not between sleep periods.

**D.** The term refers to the study protocol, not to staffing. Typically one technologist monitors the entire study.

Exam Trap

Assuming "split-night" refers to a literal split in the night's schedule (half before midnight, half after) or to electrode application, rather than to the diagnostic-to-therapeutic protocol transition.

Memory Anchor

Split-night = diagnostic portion first, CPAP titration second (if criteria met). Two purposes, one night.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
During CPAP titration, a technologist observes that the inspiratory portion of the airflow signal appears flattened or "scooped" despite the absence of frank apneas or hypopneas. The patient has no significant mask leak.

What does this finding indicate?

options.text: Flow limitation or inspiratory flattening, suggesting that upper airway resistance is still present and the pressure may need to be increased further to achieve optimal therapy.
The pressure is too high and is distorting the airflow waveform.
The patient has developed central sleep apnea.
The airflow sensor is incorrectly calibrated.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Inspiratory flow limitation appears on the airflow signal as a flattened or "scooped" inspiratory waveform contour, indicating that the upper airway is partially narrowed during inspiration despite the absence of frank apneas or hypopneas. This finding means the current pressure is not fully stenting the airway — residual upper airway resistance is present. Increasing CPAP pressure can further dilate the airway, restore a rounded inspiratory waveform, and optimize therapy. Flow limitation is an important titration target beyond simply eliminating apneas and hypopneas.

**Clue in the question.** "Scooped" or "flattened" inspiratory waveform without apneas/hypopneas, good mask fit — the classic description of flow limitation.

Domain 4: Treatment and Intervention — Recognition and management of flow limitation during CPAP titration
rationales.eli10:
Even when the airway is not fully closing, it can still be too narrow — like a garden hose that is partially kinked. The airflow signal on CPAP should look like a smooth rounded hump during breathing in. If it looks flat or scooped out on top, the airway is still being squeezed. The pressure needs to go up a bit more to fully open the passage.

ELI Example

Like a partially blocked straw — liquid still comes through, but you have to work harder. A fully open straw lets liquid flow easily with a round, smooth flow.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** Flow limitation indicates the pressure is too low to fully stent the airway (persistent upper airway resistance), not that it is too high.

**C.** Central sleep apnea involves absent respiratory effort and is not characterized by flow limitation waveforms.

**D.** The finding is a real physiological signal (flow limitation), not a calibration error. The waveform shape provides clinically actionable information.

Exam Trap

Assuming that because apneas and hypopneas are absent, the current pressure is adequate. Flow limitation is a distinct indicator of residual upper airway obstruction that warrants further pressure increase.

Memory Anchor

Flattened inspiratory waveform = flow limitation = upper airway resistance = increase CPAP pressure.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A respiratory event during an adult PSG shows an initial period of absent airflow with no respiratory effort (central component), followed by a period of absent airflow with increasing respiratory effort (obstructive component).

How should this event be classified?

options.text: Obstructive apnea
Central apnea
Hypopnea
Mixed apnea

rationales.whyCorrect:
A mixed apnea is defined by an initial central component (absent airflow with no respiratory effort) followed by an obstructive component (absent airflow with increasing respiratory effort). The event described matches this definition exactly: it begins with no effort (central), then transitions to increasing effort while airflow remains absent (obstructive). Mixed apneas are distinct from purely obstructive or purely central events and are scored as a separate category. They are particularly important in the context of therapy-emergent events during PAP titration.

**Clue in the question.** The two-phase description — initial period with no effort (central), followed by period with increasing effort (obstructive) — is the defining sequence of a mixed apnea.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, Data Verification — Classification of mixed apneas
rationales.eli10:
A mixed apnea is like a two-part problem. First, the brain briefly "forgets" to tell the lungs to breathe (central part). Then, the brain starts trying again but the throat is blocked (obstructive part). The patient has no airflow during both parts — first because they are not trying, then because they are trying but the airway is closed.

ELI Example

Like a car that will not start — first the battery is dead (central: no signal), then after you jump-start it, the engine is flooded (obstructive: trying but blocked).

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Obstructive apnea has continued or increased effort throughout the entire event — not an initial period of absent effort.

**B.** Central apnea has absent effort throughout the entire event — not a transition to increasing effort.

**C.** Hypopnea is a partial reduction (≥30%, not ≥90%), not a complete cessation of airflow.

Exam Trap

Scoring a mixed apnea as purely obstructive because effort is present at the end, ignoring the initial central component. Both phases must be recognized for correct classification.

Memory Anchor

Mixed apnea = central component first (no effort) + obstructive component second (effort resumes). Two phases, one event.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A technologist is placing respiratory effort belts on an obese patient. During calibration, the abdominal effort signal appears very low in amplitude compared to the thoracic effort signal.

What is the MOST appropriate adjustment?

options.text: Reposition the abdominal belt to the point of maximal excursion and verify adequate tension; in obese patients, the belt may perform better when placed over the umbilicus rather than below it.
Increase the gain on the thoracic channel to match the abdominal channel.
Remove the abdominal belt and use the thoracic belt alone.
Switch to a nasal pressure transducer for effort measurement.

rationales.whyCorrect:
In obese patients, abdominal wall anatomy differs from lean patients — the point of maximal respiratory excursion is often higher, near or above the umbilicus, rather than below it. A belt placed below the abdominal pannus may detect minimal movement. The appropriate troubleshooting approach is to reposition the belt to the area of greatest visible excursion during breathing and verify tension is adequate (not too loose or too tight). Increasing gain on the thoracic channel does not fix a poorly positioned abdominal belt.

**Clue in the question.** The patient is obese and the abdominal signal is specifically low relative to the thoracic signal — a placement issue, not an electronic one.

Domain 2: Study Preparation and Performance — Respiratory effort belt placement and optimization
rationales.eli10:
On larger patients, the breathing movement can happen higher up on the belly than expected. If the belt is placed too low, it misses most of the motion. The technologist should watch where the belly moves the most when the patient breathes and put the belt right there — which is often right over the belly button on bigger patients.

ELI Example

Like placing a microphone — you need to put it where the sound is loudest, not just anywhere on the stage.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** Increasing the gain on the thoracic channel does not improve the abdominal signal; it creates an artificial amplitude mismatch without addressing the underlying placement issue.

**C.** Removing the abdominal belt entirely would lose respiratory effort information and is not consistent with standard PSG montage requirements.

**D.** Nasal pressure transducers measure airflow, not respiratory effort. These are different physiological signals, and one cannot substitute for the other.

Exam Trap

Assuming the solution is electronic (increasing gain) rather than mechanical (repositioning the sensor). In PSG troubleshooting, always optimize sensor placement before adjusting electronic settings.

Memory Anchor

Obesity + low abdominal effort signal = reposition belt to umbilicus (point of maximal excursion). Fix placement, not gain.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A patient with a history of claustrophobia arrives for their first CPAP titration study. They become visibly anxious when shown the CPAP mask during the pre-study setup.

What is the FIRST step the technologist should take?

options.text: Tell the patient they can go home and reschedule when they feel ready.
Apply the mask quickly so the patient does not have time to think about it.
Begin the study without PAP and convert to a diagnostic study only.
Allow the patient to hold and handle the mask, practice breathing with it while awake, and use desensitization techniques before the study begins.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Desensitization is the evidence-based first-line behavioral approach for CPAP-related claustrophobia. Allowing the patient to handle the mask, practice wearing it while awake, and gradually acclimate to the sensation of pressure builds familiarity and reduces anxiety. This approach can be supplemented with relaxation techniques. Rushing mask application, dismissing the patient, or converting the study without attempting desensitization are all suboptimal approaches that fail to address the patient's needs.

**Clue in the question.** Patient has "a history of claustrophobia" and becomes "visibly anxious" — the FIRST step should be behavioral desensitization, not avoidance.

Domain 1: Clinical Overview, Education, Patient Support — Managing CPAP-related claustrophobia through desensitization
rationales.eli10:
Some people feel trapped or panicked when something is placed over their face. The best way to help is to go slowly: let them touch the mask, hold it to their face without the straps, then wear it for short periods while they are awake. This step-by-step approach helps their brain learn that the mask is safe. Jumping straight to full application makes the fear worse.

ELI Example

Like getting into a cold swimming pool — you dip your toes first, then wade in gradually, rather than cannonballing into the deep end.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Sending the patient home without any desensitization attempt abandons their clinical need and delays necessary treatment.

**B.** Rapid mask application in a claustrophobic patient is likely to trigger a panic response, reinforcing the fear and potentially compromising the study.

**C.** Converting to a diagnostic-only study might be a backup plan but should not be the first step — desensitization should be attempted first.

Exam Trap

Choosing to send the patient home (A) as a "safe" option rather than recognizing that desensitization is the appropriate clinical intervention. Technologists have a role in helping patients overcome PAP-related anxiety.

Memory Anchor

Claustrophobia + CPAP = desensitization. Let patient handle mask, practice awake, gradual acclimation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A patient being titrated on auto-adjusting PAP (APAP) is noted to have a large, persistent mouth leak despite using a nasal mask interface. The device pressure has escalated to the maximum set limit, but events persist.

What is the MOST appropriate intervention?

options.text: Increase the maximum pressure limit on the APAP device.
Add a chinstrap without changing the mask.
Continue with the current setup and document the finding.

Address the mouth leak by switching to an oronasal (full-face) mask or adding an effective chinstrap, as mouth leak can cause the APAP device to misinterpret leak as flow limitation and escalate pressure inappropriately.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Mouth leak during nasal PAP therapy creates a significant problem with auto-adjusting algorithms: the device cannot distinguish between leak and patient airflow. Large mouth leaks can be misinterpreted as flow limitation, causing the APAP device to escalate pressure to its maximum limit — the very scenario described. The appropriate intervention is to address the mouth leak directly, either by switching to an oronasal (full-face) mask that covers both nose and mouth, or by adding a chinstrap. Increasing the pressure limit would only worsen the problem.

**Clue in the question.** Large persistent mouth leak + APAP escalated to maximum + events persist — this is the classic APAP mouth leak vicious cycle.

Domain 4: Treatment and Intervention — Mouth leak management during auto-PAP titration
rationales.eli10:
When a patient breathes out through their mouth while using a nose-only CPAP mask, the machine gets confused — it thinks all that escaping air means the airway is collapsing. So it cranks up the pressure higher and higher, trying to fix a problem that is actually caused by the mouth leak. The solution is to stop the mouth leak, either by switching to a mask that covers both nose and mouth or by using a chin strap to keep the mouth closed.

ELI Example

Like a thermostat next to an open window — it keeps turning up the heat because it feels cold air, but the real problem is the window, not the temperature setting.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Increasing the maximum pressure limit makes the problem worse — the device will simply escalate further in response to the misidentified leak signal.

**B.** Adding a chinstrap alone may be insufficient if mouth breathing persists; however, this is mentioned in the correct answer alongside the mask switch as an option.

**C.** Continuing without intervention allows the inappropriate pressure escalation to continue and does not achieve effective therapy.

Exam Trap

Assuming that because the APAP device is escalating pressure, the patient needs more pressure. Always evaluate for mouth leak when APAP pressures are unexpectedly high.

Memory Anchor

APAP + high pressure + persistent events = suspect mouth leak. Fix leak with full-face mask or chinstrap before adjusting pressure settings.

subjectWideQuestions.stem: A technologist is scoring periodic limb movements during sleep (PLMS). An individual leg movement must meet which amplitude criterion relative to the resting baseline EMG amplitude?

options.text: An increase of at least 4 microvolts from baseline.
An increase of at least 8 microvolts from baseline.
An increase of at least 15 microvolts from baseline.
Any visible increase from baseline regardless of amplitude.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Per AASM scoring rules, a leg movement (LM) is defined as an increase in anterior tibialis EMG amplitude of at least 8 microvolts above the resting baseline EMG amplitude, lasting between 0.5 and 10 seconds. This amplitude criterion is essential to distinguish clinically significant movements from minor muscle twitches or background EMG fluctuations. The 8-microvolt threshold is specifically stated in the AASM manual for scoring periodic limb movements during sleep (PLMS).

**Clue in the question.** The question specifically asks for the "amplitude criterion" for individual leg movements relative to resting baseline — a direct rule recall question.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, Data Verification — Periodic limb movement scoring criteria
rationales.eli10:
The leg movement sensors pick up muscle activity. To count as a real leg movement (not just random muscle twitching), the electrical signal from the leg muscle must jump up by at least 8 millionths of a volt (microvolts) above the resting level. Think of it like a minimum height requirement for a wave to be counted as a wave.

ELI Example

Like a minimum height requirement for a roller coaster — you have to be at least this tall (8 microvolts) to ride (count as a leg movement).

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** 4 microvolts is below the AASM threshold. Using this lower cutoff would over-count movements, including non-clinically significant activity.

**C.** 15 microvolts is too high — this would miss many clinically significant leg movements that fall between 8 and 15 microvolts.

**D.** "Any visible increase" is far too subjective and would include artifact, respiratory-related muscle activity, and other non-PLMS signals.

Exam Trap

Confusing the 8-microvolt PLM amplitude criterion with other amplitude thresholds in PSG (slow wave amplitude of 75 microvolts for N3, or the 4-microvolt EEG calibration signal). The PLM criterion is specifically 8 microvolts.

Memory Anchor

PLM amplitude criterion = increase of 8 microvolts or more above resting baseline EMG.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
During the physiological calibration, a technologist asks the patient to perform a voluntary breath hold for 10 seconds.

What should the technologist observe on the recording during this maneuver?

options.text: Cessation of airflow with continued respiratory effort, confirming the ability to distinguish central from obstructive events.
A sudden increase in heart rate.
An immediate transition into Stage N1 sleep.
Cessation of airflow and respiratory effort simultaneously, demonstrating the appearance of a central apnea on the recording.

rationales.whyCorrect:
During a voluntary breath hold, the patient stops breathing by choice. This produces a simultaneous cessation of both airflow and respiratory effort — the exact pattern of a central apnea. Performing this calibration maneuver allows the technologist to verify that the respiratory effort sensors (belts) and airflow sensors are functioning properly, and provides a reference for what a central apnea looks like on that specific patient's recording. It also confirms the patient's ability to follow instructions and the integrity of the respiratory recording channels.

**Clue in the question.** "Voluntary breath hold" — the patient chooses not to breathe, which mimics a central (not obstructive) apnea.

Domain 2: Study Preparation and Performance — Physiological calibration and signal verification
rationales.eli10:
When you hold your breath on purpose, you stop breathing in (no airflow) AND your chest and belly stop moving (no effort). This is exactly what a central apnea looks like on the recording — both lines go flat at the same time. The technologist uses this to make sure the breathing sensors are working and to see what a central pause looks like for this patient.

ELI Example

Like testing a car's dashboard by turning the key to see all the warning lights come on — you are checking that the sensors register the event correctly.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** A voluntary breath hold does not produce continued respiratory effort — effort stops because the patient is intentionally not breathing. This describes an obstructive apnea calibration, which requires a different maneuver (such as an Mueller maneuver).

**B.** A breath hold may cause a mild heart rate change, but this is not the primary observation — verifying respiratory channel function is the purpose.

**C.** A breath hold during wake calibration does not induce sleep onset.

Exam Trap

Confusing the breath hold maneuver (simulates central apnea — no airflow, no effort) with an obstructive simulation maneuver (simulates obstructive apnea — no airflow, continued effort).

Memory Anchor

Voluntary breath hold = simulates central apnea (no airflow + no effort). Obstructive simulation = Mueller maneuver or similar (no airflow + effort continues).

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A patient's spouse calls the sleep laboratory the morning after the patient's study and asks, "Did my husband have sleep apnea? I need to know because I'm worried about his driving."

What is the technologist's BEST response?

options.text: Provide the AHI result since the spouse has a legitimate safety concern.
Explain that patient results are confidential and cannot be shared without the patient's written authorization; offer to have the patient call back to discuss releasing information.
Tell the spouse the results were normal to alleviate their concern.
Suggest the spouse contact the Department of Motor Vehicles directly.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Patient health information is protected under HIPAA (Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act). The technologist cannot disclose PSG results — including the AHI — to a spouse without the patient's explicit written authorization. This response correctly protects patient confidentiality while also offering a constructive path forward (having the patient call back to discuss information release). Even though the spouse's concern about driving safety is legitimate, confidentiality laws do not make exceptions for concerned family members.

**Clue in the question.** The spouse (not the patient) is calling and asking for results — a direct test of confidentiality knowledge.

Domain 1: Clinical Overview, Education, Patient Support — Patient confidentiality and HIPAA compliance
rationales.eli10:
Medical privacy laws say that a patient's test results belong to the patient — not to their spouse, even if the spouse is worried. The technologist cannot share any results without the patient's written permission. They can suggest that the patient call back and give permission to share the information, but until then, the results stay private.

ELI Example

Like a bank account — even if your spouse is worried about finances, the bank will not tell them your balance without your permission.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** This is a HIPAA violation — the spouse has no legal right to the patient's results, regardless of safety concerns.

**C.** Falsifying results (saying they are normal when the technologist may not even know the result) is dishonest and unethical.

**D.** This deflects the issue without addressing confidentiality and inappropriately involves a third party (DMV).

Exam Trap

Rationalizing a confidentiality breach because the spouse's concern seems legitimate (driving safety). HIPAA does not make exceptions for well-intentioned disclosures to family members without patient authorization.

Memory Anchor

Never release patient results to family without written authorization. HIPAA applies to everyone, even spouses.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A technologist is preparing to initiate CPAP titration on a pediatric patient (age 10, weight 35 kg) with severe OSA (diagnostic AHI 30 events/hour).

What is the recommended starting CPAP pressure for pediatric titration?

options.text: 10 cm H₂O, the same as for adults with severe OSA.
15 cm H₂O, because pediatric OSA is more severe.
4 cm H₂O, with gradual increases as tolerated; pediatric patients often start at the lowest pressure to allow for acclimation.
The pressure determined by the patient's weight in kilograms divided by 5.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Pediatric CPAP titration follows different protocols than adult titration. Children often start at 4 cm H₂O (the lowest standard CPAP setting) to allow gradual acclimation to the sensation of pressure. Pediatric patients may be more sensitive to pressure and more anxious about the mask. Starting low and titrating slowly reduces the risk of intolerance and treatment refusal. The severity of the diagnostic AHI does not change the recommended starting pressure — adequate titration is achieved through systematic increases, not by starting high.

**Clue in the question.** The patient is a 10-year-old child — pediatric protocols differ from adult protocols.

Domain 4: Treatment and Intervention — Pediatric CPAP titration
rationales.eli10:
Children need a gentler start with CPAP. Instead of starting at a higher pressure (like many adults), the technologist starts at the lowest setting — just 4 cm H₂O — and slowly turns it up as the child gets comfortable. This prevents the child from becoming scared or refusing treatment. Even if the child has severe sleep apnea, starting low and going slow is the right approach.

ELI Example

Like introducing a child to swimming — you start in the shallow end, not by throwing them into the deep end.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** 10 cm H₂O is too high as a starting pressure for a pediatric patient, regardless of OSA severity. Adult starting pressures do not apply to children.

**B.** 15 cm H₂O is excessively high for any starting pressure, especially in pediatrics.

**D.** Weight-based pressure formulas are not used for pediatric CPAP titration — pressure is titrated based on observed response.

Exam Trap

Applying adult CPAP titration protocols to pediatric patients. Pediatric patients require different starting pressures and a more gradual titration approach.

Memory Anchor

Pediatric CPAP start = 4 cm H₂O. Gradual titration upward. Lowest pressure first for acclimation.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A technologist is scoring PLMS and identifies a series of four consecutive leg movements. The intervals between the onset of successive movements are 12 seconds, 8 seconds, and 32 seconds.

Which statement about this series is correct?

options.text: All four movements constitute a valid PLM series, as there are at least four consecutive movements with all inter-movement intervals falling within the 5-90 second range.
The series is invalid because at least five movements are required.
Only the first two movements form a PLM series because the third interval exceeds 30 seconds.
The series is invalid because the intervals are not uniform.

rationales.whyCorrect:
Per AASM rules, a PLM series requires at least four consecutive leg movements, with each inter-movement interval (the time from the onset of one movement to the onset of the next) falling between 5 and 90 seconds. The intervals described are 12 seconds, 8 seconds, and 32 seconds — all fall within the 5-90 second window. With four movements and three intervals all between 5-90 seconds, this meets the criteria for a valid PLM series. The intervals do not need to be uniform.

**Clue in the question.** The intervals given (12, 8, 32 seconds) must be checked against the 5-90 second rule — all three fall within range.

Domain 3: Scoring, Reporting, Data Verification — PLM series scoring criteria
rationales.eli10:
For leg movements to count as a "periodic" series (PLMS), there must be at least four kicks in a row, with each kick coming between 5 and 90 seconds after the previous one. The kicks do not have to be evenly spaced — 12 seconds, then 8 seconds, then 32 seconds is fine, as long as all gaps are between 5 and 90 seconds. All three gaps qualify, so all four kicks form a valid series.

ELI Example

Like a train — you need at least four cars (movements), and the gaps between cars (intervals) must be within a certain range. The gaps do not all have to be the same size.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**B.** The minimum number for a PLM series is four movements, not five. Four movements with three qualifying intervals meets criteria.

**C.** The third interval (32 seconds) is within the 5-90 second range — the upper limit is 90 seconds, not 30 seconds.

**D.** Inter-movement intervals do not need to be uniform — variability in the intervals is expected in PLMS.

Exam Trap

Confusing the minimum number of movements (four) with five, or misunderstanding the upper interval limit as 30 seconds instead of 90 seconds.

Memory Anchor

PLM series = ≥4 movements, inter-movement intervals 5-90 seconds. Intervals need not be uniform.

subjectWideQuestions.stem:
A technologist is preparing a patient for an MSLT (Multiple Sleep Latency Test). The patient asks whether they can have coffee before the first nap.

What is the MOST appropriate response?

options.text: "Yes, but only one cup before the first nap."
"Caffeine and other stimulants should be avoided during the MSLT, as they can affect sleep latency and invalidate the test results."
"You may have coffee, but only between naps."
"Only decaffeinated coffee is permitted during the MSLT."

rationales.whyCorrect:
The MSLT measures the patient's propensity to fall asleep under standardized conditions. Caffeine is a central nervous system stimulant that increases sleep latency and may prevent sleep onset during nap opportunities. Consuming caffeine during the MSLT would artificially prolong sleep latency, potentially masking pathological sleepiness and invalidating the test. The MSLT protocol specifically requires that stimulants be avoided during the test day. Decaffeinated coffee still contains trace amounts of caffeine and is not recommended.

**Clue in the question.** The patient asks about coffee before an MSLT nap — caffeine directly interferes with the test's purpose (measuring sleepiness).

Domain 1: Clinical Overview, Education, Patient Support — MSLT protocol patient education
rationales.eli10:
The MSLT measures how quickly you fall asleep during the day. Caffeine keeps you awake — that is why people drink it. Having caffeine during the test would be like cheating on the measurement; it would make you seem less sleepy than you really are, which could lead to a missed diagnosis. The test only works if you avoid anything that fights sleepiness.

ELI Example

Like trying to measure how fast a car can go while also pressing the brakes — caffeine is the brake, and you need it completely off to get an accurate measurement.

Why the Other Choices Are Wrong

**A.** Allowing any caffeine, even a single cup, can affect MSLT results and is not permitted.

**C.** Caffeine between naps still affects subsequent nap latencies and is not permitted at any time during the MSLT day.

**D.** Decaffeinated coffee still contains small amounts of caffeine and is not recommended during the MSLT.

Exam Trap

Thinking that "just one cup" or "only decaf" is acceptable during the MSLT. The protocol requires complete avoidance of stimulants during the test day.

Memory Anchor

MSLT protocol = no caffeine, no stimulants during the entire test day. They artificially increase sleep latency.
